Populations with identical AI adoption and average skill can differ sharply: when strategies change frequently, skills remain homogeneous and collective lock-in to high AI adoption is stronger; when strategies persist, lock-in weakens but the population can polarize into highly skilled autonomous workers and AI-dependent individuals. Modeling output overlap further shows that more diverse AI outputs can make widespread adoption harder to reverse. Together, these results expose tradeoffs between the benefits of widespread AI adoption and its long-run risks, making collective lock-in and skill polarization distinct intervention targets.

Introduction. The modern system of medical education is undergoing active transformation under the influence of globalization, rapid development of medical technologies, and the digitalization of the educational process. The implementation of innovative approaches, including simulation-based learning, artificial intelligence technologies, as well as virtual and augmented reality, contributes to improving the effectiveness of training medical professionals. At the same time, the intensification of the educational process and the digitalization of the learning environment may affect the psycho-emotional state and health of participants in the educational process, which determines the need to analyze current pedagogical trends in medical education. Aim. To analyze modern pedagogical trends in medical education and determine their impact on learning effectiveness and the health of participants in the educational process. Materials and methods. An analytical review of scientific publications by domestic and foreign authors devoted to the development of medical education, the implementation of digital technologies in the educational process, and studies examining the influence of the educational environment on the psycho-emotional state of students and teachers was conducted. Methods of system analysis, generalization, and comparison of the results of contemporary scientific research were used. Results. It was established that the integration of innovative educational technologies contributes to improving the quality of training of medical professionals, the development of clinical thinking, and the formation of practical skills. At the same time, the increasing academic workload, the digital intensity of the educational process, and the need for continuous professional development may lead to higher levels of stress, emotional exhaustion, and professional burnout among participants in the educational process. Conclusions. Modern medical education requires a balanced combination of innovative pedagogical technologies and approaches aimed at preserving the mental and physical health of participants in the educational process. A promising direction is the development of health-preserving educational strategies, optimization of academic workload, and the implementation of trauma-informed approaches in the system of medical education.

Massive alarm data from grid monitoring systems is essential for secure power dispatch operation. Aggregating discrete alarm signals into structured events is vital to enhance grid monitoring intelligence. Nevertheless, existing event rule bases adopt domain-customized complex grammar with diverse symbolic expressions, making traditional string matching methods unable to achieve accurate semantic parsing. This paper proposes a multi-agent collaboration-based method for semantic recognition and real-time generation of power grid monitoring alarm events. The method integrates large language models (LLMs), knowledge graph (KG) representation learning, and multi-agent coordination to realize high-precision semantic understanding and real-time intelligent generation of alarm events. Specifically, three original contributions are made: (1) a three-layer standardized preprocessing pipeline combined with instruction tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that bridges the semantic gap between domain-specific rule grammar and LLMs; (2) a dual-drive fusion recognition model integrating GraphSAGE-based knowledge graph embedding and BiLSTM temporal encoding with an attention fusion mechanism; and (3) a hierarchical multi-agent collaborative architecture with explicit communication protocols, conflict resolution strategies, and a SEEN (Semantic Event Exception Notifier) algorithm for unknown event detection. Experimental results on 356,950 real alarm samples from a regional power grid demonstrate that the proposed method achieves an F1-score of 96.9% and a false alarm rate of 4.2%, outperforming conventional rule matching methods by 25.3% points under signal-loss scenarios. Ablation studies confirm that each module contributes independently and significantly to the overall performance.

Open radio access network (O-RAN) enables a multi-vendor ecosystem that accelerates xApp development for near-real-time (RT) network management. However, this openness shifts a combinatorial coordination burden to the Non-RT layer, where rApp policies compose xApps from a growing catalog to realize operator intents. Coexisting intents further compound this challenge, as conflicts may arise among xApp actions, rApp policies, and their cross-layer interactions. To maximize intent admission while maintaining key performance indicator (KPI) compliance across incoming and incumbent intents, we propose a large language model-based Multi-Agentic AI framework. A Reasoning Agent screens candidate xApps against KPI contracts and produces a joint intent admission and xApp assignment decision. On post-deployment KPI violations, a Diagnosis Agent identifies the root causes of failure, labels the conflict mechanism, and guides the Reasoning Agent in subsequent attempts. Experimental results show that the framework based on GPT-OSS 120B achieves 28.6% more KPI-compliant cases and admits over 15* as many incoming intents as state-of-the-art baselines. Under the Qwen 72B variant, Diagnosis increases compliant cases by 50.0%, quadruples admitted intents, and reduces deployment attempts by 32.6%. A live deployment conforming to O-RAN specifications further validates the feasibility of the proposed solution for conflict-aware rApp policy orchestration in real networks.

Accurate vessel trajectory prediction is essential for maritime situational awareness, traffic management, and autonomous navigation. However, existing data-driven methods often struggle to simultaneously represent temporal dependencies at different scales, nonlinear maneuver-induced deviations, and kinematic consistency, particularly as the forecasting horizon increases. This study proposes TCN–KAN–PINN, a unified framework combining a multi-scale causal Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN), a parallel Linear-KAN predictor, and physics-informed training. The TCN encoder uses hierarchical dilated residual blocks and sample-specific scale fusion to extract complementary temporal features from historical AIS observations. The Linear Base Pathway models the dominant motion trend, whereas the KAN Residual Pathway learns nonlinear corrections associated with vessel maneuvers. A time-discretized kinematic residual further penalizes discrepancies between predicted coordinate increments and expected displacements derived from vessel motion states, while Relative Loss Balancing with Random Lookback (ReLoBRaLo) adaptively balances the data and physics objectives. The model directly generates a complete 30-step future trajectory, with the 5 min, 15 min, and 30 min results evaluated as prefixes of the same output. Experiments on a real-world AIS dataset show that the proposed framework achieves the best overall trajectory accuracy among representative kinematic and deep learning baselines while maintaining favorable speed and course consistency and practical inference efficiency. Results reported as mean ± standard deviation over five independent runs indicate stable predictive performance. Ablation studies further show that kinematic supervision benefits prediction from the early forecasting steps, whereas the contribution of the KAN pathway becomes more pronounced at medium and long horizons.

The prediction of software defects is important to detect defects in source codes prior to their deployment but traditional techniques use selected features and limited binary classification. This research work proposes DefectGuard, a transformer-based multiclass software defect prediction system for C/C++ source code that utilizes CodeBERT fine-tuning. This custom dataset consists of 2,000 samples of manually collected and labeled C/C++ source codes and includes nine classes of defects, namely syntax, semantic, logic, linker, and runtime-related defects. The proposed pipeline includes preprocessing, stratified splitting, sub-word tokenization, CodeBERT representation learning, and multiclass classification. The experimental results show the accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score of 98.8%, 96.4%, 95.8%, and 96.1%, respectively, on the test set. Additionally, ROC-AUC and confusion-matrix metrics are used to evaluate the class-level discrimination. Moreover, the proposed model is implemented in a real-time Flask-based web application, which can classify the source code into defect labels with confidence scores and language detection to provide the interpretation feedback.

The rapid growth of multilingual digital communication has created an urgent need for efficient Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems capable of handling diverse linguistic structures. While modern NLP approaches are increasingly dominated by data-driven and deep learning techniques, linguistic frameworks continue to play a significant role in enhancing language understanding. Among such frameworks, Paninian Grammar, developed by the ancient Indian grammarian Panini, has emerged as a valuable theoretical foundation for multilingual language processing, particularly in morphologically rich and free word-order languages. Paninian Grammar offers a rule-based, dependency-oriented model that focuses on semantic and syntactic relationships among linguistic elements. Its concepts such as Karaka relations, dependency structures, and grammatical transformations provide an effective mechanism for computational analysis of Indian languages and other morphologically complex languages. Over the past few decades, researchers have utilized Paninian principles in machine translation, parsing, information extraction, and multilingual language technologies. Despite its strengths, the application of Paninian Grammar in multilingual language processing faces several challenges, including linguistic diversity, ambiguity resolution, scalability issues, integration with modern neural architectures, and the scarcity of annotated corpora. This paper examines the role of Paninian Grammar in multilingual language processing, discusses its computational significance, analyzes major challenges, and explores future research directions aimed at integrating traditional linguistic knowledge with contemporary artificial intelligence technologies.

Abstract The European Association of Urology (EAU) risk groups guide treatment decisions in prostate cancer using prostate-specific antigen (PSA), ISUP grade, and clinical stage, but do not incorporate histopathological image information. We evaluated a locked multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) model that integrates routinely available clinical variables (age, PSA, and ISUP grade) with deep-learning features extracted from diagnostic biopsy whole-slide images for predicting outcomes after radiotherapy (RT). The model was originally trained to predict biochemical recurrence (BCR) following radical prostatectomy and was applied without retraining to 353 patients from the population-based STHLM3 trial (ISRCTN84445406) treated with RT. Study endpoints included BCR (Phoenix definition), high-risk BCR (HR-BCR), and prostate cancer-specific mortality (PCSM). Model performance was assessed using Harrell’s C-index and cumulative incidence analyses and compared with EAU risk groups. The continuous AI score showed C-indices of 0.65 (95% CI 0.55–0.74) for BCR, 0.84 (0.72–0.95) for HR-BCR, and 0.81 (0.63–1.00) for PCSM, compared with 0.60, 0.82, and 0.80, respectively, for EAU risk groups. Although paired differences in C-index between AI and EAU were not statistically significant, adding the continuous AI score to EAU classification improved model fit for BCR, HR-BCR, and PCSM. Exploratory AI risk stratification classified 18.9% of EAU intermediate-risk patients as AI high-risk and 28.2% of EAU high-risk patients as AI low-risk. Within the EAU high-risk group, patients classified as AI low-risk ( n = 24) experienced no BCR events during 10 years of follow-up, compared with a 10-year cumulative incidence of 28.7% (95% CI 17.3–41.2%) among AI high-risk patients ( n = 61). These findings suggest that multimodal AI may refine EAU risk stratification by identifying distinct prognostic subgroups within established risk categories, although prospective validation is needed before its potential role in individualized treatment decision-making can be established.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Hind A Alsudays,1 Sultanah Alsudays21Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Majmaah University, Al Majmaah, 11952, Saudi Arabia; 2Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), Riyadh, Saudi ArabiaCorrespondence: Sultanah Alsudays, Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Email Smalsudays@imamu.edu.saPurpose: This quantitative study examined the relationships between perceived organizational support (POS), Artificial intelligence self-efficacy (AISE), employees’ artificial intelligence learning anxiety (AILA), and AI job replacement anxiety (AIJRA) in private sector employees; it examined the potential direct effect of POS on both AILA and AIJRA, and the indirect effect via AISE by drawing on social cognitive theory and using structural equation modeling (SEM).Participants and Methods: Convenience and snowball sampling techniques were used to recruit 311 employees from the private sector in the Saudi context. Data were collected using an online survey and analyzed using Mplus to conduct confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and SEM.Results: In the total sample, POS influences AI learning anxiety only via AI self-efficacy (β = - 0.073; p ≤ 0.01). However, AI job replacement anxiety was influenced only directly by POS (β = − 0.184; p ≤ 0.01). These findings suggest that the relative importance of organizational and individual factors varies based on the type of AI anxiety. Finally, Age has a significant and negative relationship with AIJRA (β = − 0.121, P ≤ 0.05).Conclusion: The Study’s findings underscore the importance of individual factors such as AISE in enhancing the role of POS on AILA. Furthermore, These findings suggest that the relative importance of organizational and individual factors varies based on the type of AI anxiety.Keywords: perceived organizational support, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, artificial intelligence learning anxiety, artificial intelligence job replacement anxiety, social cognitive theory, Saudi private sector

Module Description This module combines open pedagogy, renewable assignments, reflective practice, AI literacy, collaborative learning, student-generated knowledge, peer review, open licensing, and repository-based dissemination, based on the Repositories of AI Literacy Resources (RAILR) concept. The module is primarily designed for undergraduate students, although it can be adapted for other educational levels depending on the instructor's teaching goals. It can be delivered as a standalone module, an elective, or with its learning activities incorporated into an existing course. The central purpose of the module is to move students beyond being consumers of AI literacy guidance resources to becoming creators. Through reflection on their own experiences of using generative AI tools, discussion with peers, collaborative resource development, peer review, and open dissemination, students can develop AI literacy resources that can benefit other learners. Instructors are not required to treat every activity as compulsory, except when implementing the module as a full course or an elective. Instead, instructors can select and adapt the activities according to their course objectives, teaching goals, available teaching time, student numbers, and preferred or feasible mode of delivery. Learning Outcomes By the end of this module, students should be able to: Explain the concept of open pedagogy and distinguish it from traditional approaches to teaching and learning. Explain the relationship between open pedagogy and renewable assignments. Differentiate between disposable and renewable assignments. Explain AI literacy Describe the importance of AI literacy for the responsible use of generative AI tools. Critically reflect on their own experiences using generative AI tools. Learn from the experiences of other students through collaborative activities. Transform personal and shared experiences into AI literacy resources. Collaboratively develop AI literacy resources suitable for open dissemination. Develop AI literacy resources for dissemination through Repositories of AI Literacy Resources (RAILR). Target Audience Level: Undergraduate Adaptable for other levels depending on instructors' teaching goals. Suitable as a standalone module or as an elective Module Outline This module is organised into the following sections: Section 1: Purpose of This Module Section 2: Open Pedagogy: From Disposable Assignments to Shared Knowledge Section 3: Learning from Experience: Why Students' Experiences with Generative AI Tools Matter Section 4: From Reflection to Resource Creation: Transforming Experience into AI Literacy Resources Section 5: Repository-Based Knowledge Sharing: Preserving and Disseminating Student-Created AI Literacy Resources in RAILR Section 6: Reflecting on Your AI Journey: Learning Through Personal Experience Section 7: Practical Learning Activities Practical Activity 1: My AI Journey Practical Activity 2: Learning from Others Practical Activity 3: Co-Creating an AI Literacy Resource Practical Activity 4: Peer Review, Improvement, and Dissemination Practical Activity 5: Complete the Appropriate RAILR Dissemination Agreement Practical Activity 6: Open Dissemination of AI Literacy Resources Section 8. Learning and Reading Resources Assessment Students will complete a series of reflective, collaborative, and resource-development activities. Depending on the instructor's implementation of the module, assessment may include: An individual reflective essay. Participation in collaborative group discussions. Development of a group AI literacy resource. Peer review of another group's AI literacy resource. Preparation of resources for dissemination through RAILR

Fine-tuning directly on user-side data is an effective way to improve the performance of widely adopted data-driven human mesh recovery (HMR) models. However, doing so for existing HMR methods often assumes aggregating user-side data from real-world HMR-deployed devices to a central training server, posing a significant privacy risk as sensitive human images are transmitted. How can human mesh recovery be evaluated and improved in privacy-constrained real-world settings? We study this question through a benchmark in which state-of-the-art HMR models are trained with federated learning and a secure-aggregation variant, neither of which centralizes raw images, and evaluated across a wide range of client-scale and data-heterogeneity settings. We document that common HMR training pipelines are built around centralized data access and quantify how representative HMR backbones behave when that assumption is removed. Furthermore, to study the data bottleneck of privacy-constrained HMR training, we propose DePoser, a local annotation and fine-tuning pipeline enhanced with depth foundation models, with which collaboratively trained HMR models can be locally tailored to the end user's distribution. On in-the-wild data, fine-tuning on DePoser annotations improves personalization accuracy, measured against DePoser-generated pseudo-ground truth. This benchmark aims to support future work on privacy-constrained HMR models and their real-world deployment and evaluation.

Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis hubungan antara pemanfaatan Artificial Intelligence (AI) dan employee engagement pada karyawan Generasi Z di era transformasi digital. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan data kuesioner daring. Sebanyak 42 respons terkumpul; 36 responden menyatakan pernah menggunakan AI untuk membantu pekerjaan dan dianalisis, sedangkan 6 responden yang tidak pernah menggunakan AI tidak dimasukkan ke analisis utama. Instrumen terdiri atas 15 butir pemanfaatan AI dan 13 butir employee engagement dengan skala Likert lima poin. Hasil penghitungan data asli menunjukkan Cronbach’s alpha sebesar 0.989 untuk pemanfaatan AI dan 0.990 untuk employee engagement. Korelasi Pearson menunjukkan hubungan positif yang kuat dan signifikan (r = 0.835; p < 0,001). Regresi linear sederhana menghasilkan persamaan Y = 0.731 + 0.819X dengan R² = 0.697; koefisien regresi signifikan, t(34) = 8.842; p < 0,001. Hasil ini menunjukkan bahwa pada sampel yang dianalisis, skor pemanfaatan AI yang lebih tinggi berkaitan dengan skor employee engagement yang lebih tinggi. Temuan perlu ditafsirkan secara hati-hati karena menggunakan sampel terbatas dan desain survei yang tidak dapat memastikan hubungan sebab-akibat.

The implementation of the government’s Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG) is an example of a policy aimed at improving the quality of human capital by meeting students’ nutritional needsa factor linked to psychological aspects such as intrinsic motivation and enthusiasm for learning. This study specifically examines the role of the MBG Program in enhancing students’ intrinsic motivation and enthusiasm for learning. A quantitative method with a correlational design was applied, involving 220 junior high school students who had participated in the MBG Program and were purposively selected for this study. Data were collected using a questionnaire that covered perceptions of the MBG Program, intrinsic motivation, and enthusiasm for learning, which had undergone validation and reliability testing. The data were statistically analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlation, and linear regression. The results of the study indicate that the participants’ perceptions of the MBG Program (M = 4.05), intrinsic motivation (M = 3.92), and enthusiasm for learning (M = 3.85) fell into the high category. The MBG Program was positively correlated with students’ intrinsic motivation (r = 0.58) and enthusiasm for learning (r = 0.52), and there was a strong correlation between intrinsic motivation and enthusiasm for learning (r = 0.71). Regression analysis showed that the MBG Program had a significant direct effect on learning enthusiasm (β = 0.21; p = 0.001) and an indirect effect mediated by intrinsic motivation (β = 0.58; p < 0.001), and explained 55.2% of the variance in learning enthusiasm (R² = 0.552). Thus, it can be concluded that the MBG Program is crucial for the development of students’ non-cognitive aspects, both directly and indirectly through the enhancement of intrinsic motivation; therefore, this program warrants the attention of education policymakers.

BACKGROUND: Evaluating how appropriate current large language models (LLMs) respond to common pediatric infectious disease (PID) questions is important for understanding their potential role in education and clinical support. Therefore, we evaluated and compared the clinical quality of answers produced by different LLMs when given professionally written, clinician-style case descriptions, using a purpose-built multi-domain evaluation tool. METHODS: Three different LLMs, including DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, ChatGPT-5, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, were investigated using 12 relevant PID scenarios. Each scenario included five open-ended questions: etiology, clinical features, diagnostics, treatment options, and complications. Two PID specialists independently reviewed all responses using a Likert scoring tool. RESULTS: All three models received high overall scores. ChatGPT-5 achieved perfect domain scores (10.0), whereas DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp showed similarly strong results, with only minor reductions in diagnostics (9.83) and treatment (9.92). Gemini 2.5 Flash demonstrated higher variability, particularly in treatment (8.83) and diagnostics (9.75), while matching the other models in clinical findings and complications (10.0) and scoring 9.83 in etiology. However, there were no statistically significant differences across models in domain-level comparisons (all p > 0.05). In addition, model-level analyses similarly demonstrated high accuracy (6.0; 5.98; 5.85), completeness (3.0; 2.97; 2.87), and safety (1.0; 1.0; 0.97) for ChatGPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, respectively (accuracy: p = 0.074; completeness: p = 0.066; safety: p = 0.14). CONCLUSION: Current LLMs performed highly in structured, expert-reviewed PID scenarios and may assist with information organization and early-stage clinical reasoning. However, their optimal use remains within clinician-supervised workflows, where AI-generated outputs complement, rather than replace, human clinical judgment. IMPACT: Current large language models (LLMs) show consistently high-quality performance across pediatric infectious disease scenarios, with no significant differences between models. Our study adds a structured, multi-domain comparison using clinician-style cases and expert evaluation, providing detailed insights into accuracy, completeness, and safety. The findings support the use of LLMs in medical education and early clinical reasoning, while highlighting their role as clinician-supervised tools rather than replacements for clinical judgment. The results demonstrate the reliability of LLMs in organizing clinical information and identifying key diagnostic and management elements in standardized scenarios.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The case of Pooja Ramesh Singh v. J&K Bank Ltd. represents a significant ruling concerning legal technology in India. The Supreme Court has introduced a policy of zero tolerance towards hallucinated precedents and has stated that any such orders are entirely void, thus protecting the integrity of the judicial record. Since artificial intelligence tools are becoming increasingly common in legal procedures, this judgment makes sure that technology stays a secondary aid to human judgment and therefore upholds the fundamental principles of natural justice, legal accuracy, and judicial accountability.

Chapter 5 examines precarious digital labour as a constitutive condition of contemporary platform capitalism, arguing that its uneven geographies cannot be understood apart from the longer histories of colonialism, racial capitalism and the global asymmetries between North and South. Moving beyond celebratory narratives of flexibility, innovation and entrepreneurial freedom, it analyses how digitally mediated work is organized through exploitation, opacity and differential exposure to risk, especially for workers in the Global South and the marginal peripheries of the Global North. It shows how labour platforms, content moderation infrastructures and AI data supply chains depend on abundant, low-waged and frequently invisibilized labour, while reproducing older hierarchies of race, class, gender and citizenship in new technological forms. In doing so, it foregrounds how digital economies extract value not only through markets and infrastructures but through the governance of precarious bodies, outsourced vulnerability and asymmetrical regimes of regulation. Bringing together debates on platform labour, migrant labour, algorithmic management and human moderation, the chapter offers a critical account of digital precarity as historically situated and globally distributed, showing how the future of work is being built upon enduring structures of dispossession, exclusion and exploitation.

Chapter 2 fleshes out the notion of ‘precarity’ within the digital economy, particularly in relation to platformization. It examines how precarity is tethered to the emergence of the digital economy as a key infrastructure for transacting labour, organizing consumption and mediating everyday life. Beyond the conventional understanding of precarity—as a condition of social or economic vulnerability, instability and powerlessness—the chapter argues that precarity is enlarged through the technical substrates of platform architecture, through user agreements and ‘dangerous permissions’, and through forms of consumption deeply enmeshed with the datafied subject. In tracing these dynamics, the chapter shows how algorithmic management, reputational systems and opaque infrastructures intensify insecurity not only for workers in the gig and crowd economy but also for users whose everyday interactions are captured, monitored and rendered productive. It therefore positions platform precarity as both a labour condition and a broader social formation, one that links digital capitalism to surveillance, dispossession and the normalization of insecurity as an ordinary feature of contemporary life.

Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards assigns one terminal reward to an entire reasoning trajectory, obscuring how individual reasoning steps contributed to the outcome. GRPO broadcasts a group-normalized advantage to every response token, while finer-grained approaches often rely on dense auxiliary rollouts or branching schemes that can also alter the data used for policy updates. We cast the missing middle as budgeted measurement: with a limited rollout budget, which partial solutions should be evaluated, and how should their value estimates refine credit? ProbePO selects partial-solution states with a reward-free uncertainty score and estimates their expected verifier rewards under a capped continuation budget. ProbePO redistributes, rather than replaces, GRPO's trajectory-level advantage across tokens while preserving each trajectory's mean token-level advantage; probe continuations serve only as measurements. Across three DeepSeekMath and Qwen-family models spanning 1.5B-7B parameters, ProbePO consistently outperforms GRPO and achieves the highest accuracy among the four evaluated methods in 16 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. Against dense-probing VinePPO on DeepSeekMath-7B, ProbePO achieves higher accuracy on all six benchmarks with 76% less end-to-end training time.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the demand for digital competencies. In particular, the gap between women's level of artificial intelligence usage and their level of independently applying it to create professional and innovative solutions is one of the pressing issues. The purpose of this study is to develop a professional-adaptive AI education model aimed at transitioning women in Uzbekistan from basic users of artificial intelligence to creators of practical solutions. The research utilized methods of system analysis, comparative analysis, model design, and digital educational platform prototyping. The model includes identifying the user's professional field, assessing initial AI competence, forming an individual learning pathway, and providing AI training sessions and practical projects aligned with professional tasks. The SheTechAI platform was developed as a technological prototype of the model. As a result of the research, a four-stage competence model is proposed, aimed at advancing AI education from 'providing knowledge about AI' to 'solving real professional problems and creating new solutions using AI'.
topics: Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies

documents.abstract: Modern statistical model development begins with a high-level specification in an automatic differentiation framework such as PyTorch, JAX, or TensorFlow, which is then lowered to a target backend by a compiler or implemented manually by a research engineer. In this paper, we study whether frontier language models can correctly perform the latter task by generating GPU kernels from high-level benchmark specifications. We introduce a framework in which a language-model agent uses Velvet, a program verifier for imperative programs embedded in Lean, to prove semantic equivalence between a high-level specification and a generated CUDA kernel under an explicit set of assumptions. It also asks the LLM to prove thread safety and data race freedom of the generated kernel in VerCors, a deductive verifier for parallel code. Our main contribution to the formal verification of LLM- generated GPU kernels is showing that a combination of Lean automation and language-model-guided proof construction can verify a broad set of basic neural- network building blocks over floating-point values, allowing LLMs to implement semantically correct and safe kernels. In our framework, floating-point verifications never rely on compiled code and are always checked via the Lean kernel.

Background: Autonomous LLM agents increasingly operate in shared environments where behavior depends on interaction history, role allocation, local norms, authority, and group structure. Objective: This conceptual methods paper develops a psychometric operationalization of dynamic functional roles in autonomous multi-agent systems using PersonaMatrix-derived measurement principles without attributing human psychological ontology to AI. Methods: A targeted evidence synthesis (2019–2026) was conducted across AI psychometrics, dynamic multi-agent roles, collective-field modeling, norm emergence, trajectory prediction, and anthropomorphism. Peer-reviewed sources were prioritized, while current OpenAI, METR/Redwood, Anthropic, and Moltbook materials were used as primary or emerging evidence for recent agent ecosystems. Results: The framework separates output-level stability (RSI, IDS, RCS) from role-level and field-level constructs. It proposes the Functional Role Consistency Index, Role Transition Index, Agent–Field Differentiation Index, Collective Utility Index, Norm Conflict Index, Regulatory Closure Index, and Field Role Composition Vector. Three falsifiable hypotheses test whether role variables add out-of-sample predictive value for agent behavior, role transitions, and future field states. Conclusion: PersonaMatrix is positioned as a measurement architecture rather than an AI personality diagnosis. The archetypal-role hypothesis is supported only if role coding is reliable, improves prediction beyond non-archetypal baselines, and generalizes to unseen agents and independent multi-agent environments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) has heightened interest in personalizing computer assisted learning (CAL) programs to tailor their instruction to individual students. Despite the proliferation of AI-driven CAL programs, evidence for their effectiveness remains limited. We present findings from a field experiment in rural China examining whether an AI-driven personalized CAL program improves student achievement. We randomly assign 8647 students from 315 primary school classes to one of three treatment arms: (i) AI-CAL, (ii) non-personalized CAL (active control), and (iii) non-CAL educational activities (pure control). Results indicate that AI-CAL does not significantly improve achievement, with estimates precise enough to rule out non-trivial positive effects. This finding holds across the difficulty of assessment items and across the baseline achievement of students. If anything, AI-CAL might be less effective than non-personalized CAL for students in the middle tercile of baseline achievement. These findings call for caution when scaling AI-driven educational technologies.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This dataset accompanies a vignette-based evaluation of AI-generated responses to 40 simulated cardiovascular cases covering coronary artery disease, heart failure, and arrhythmias.The Excel file contains case identifiers, age, sex, disease category, clinical severity category, age group, and individual scores from three cardiologist raters across eight evaluation domains: medical accuracy, factual accuracy, completeness, clarity, urgency, language quality, absence of false claims, and absence of harm. It also includes individual Global Quality Scores (GQS), calculated mean scores, and binary harmfulness assessments.The accompanying vignette document provides the clinical scenarios used in the evaluation. Case identifiers correspond across the files, enabling linkage between each vignette and its associated ratings.All cases are simulated and contain no identifiable patient information. Column abbreviations ending in R1, R2, and R3 denote the three raters; columns ending in Mean contain the corresponding average scores.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools have spread rapidly among professionals, and experiments show substantial gains on isolated tasks. Yet average effects on earnings and recorded hours have been small, although changes in task organization are already evident. This conceptual article proposes that an important part of this gap is explained by how people represent the technology: generative AI tends to be perceived as a question-and-answer tool rather than as an executor of process steps, let alone of recurring routines that keep running while the person only checks the result. Drawing on literatures on the task-based approach in labor economics, levels of automation, trust and overreliance in automated systems, work design and redesign, sociotechnical frames, transfer of training, and habit formation, the article develops a five-element model (perception, decomposition, allocation, verification, and routinization) and argues that the relevant question shifts from “how do I ask?” to “who performs each step?”, with three possible destinations for each step: AI alone, AI with human verification, or the person. Seven testable propositions are formulated, and implications for research, training design, and organizations are discussed. The article presents no new data; its contribution is to organize dispersed evidence into an explicit, falsifiable mechanism.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: A basic mathematical foundation, as part of a knowledge-based educational framework aligned with Oman Vision 2040, could serve as the intellectual foundation for STEM development. The Mathematics course in the General Foundation Program (GFP) at the University of Technology and Applied Sciences (UTAS) is vital for students planning to pursue fields such as information technology, artificial intelligence, engineering, and data science. However, concerns remain significant as the program focuses on procedural skills and is less focused on analytical reasoning and modeling. The CDP has a digital math literacy component, but it is limited. None of the previous attempts to assess structured curriculum mapping has proven effective. Through structured curriculum mapping and a comparative readiness analysis, this study examines Course Learning Outcomes, Course Objectives, assessment plans, course delivery strategies, and proposed revisions aligned with a 10-dimensional STEM Readiness Framework. It also considers the spread of Bloom's taxonomy. The paper notes observed alignment gaps, graphically documents them, and benchmarks insights from Harvard University’s mathematics pathways against policy recommendations. Results demonstrated around 70% agreement in content but also highlighted discrepancies between evaluation and instruction in two specific areas: modeling and decision-making under uncertainty, as well as digital exploration. Even though the same applies to the requirements for using general skills for knowledge, in the higher cognitive sphere, these limitations are even more severe. Proposed revisions include strengthened analytical and practical competencies, moving from bridge to cognitive enhancement. Advancing IT and engineering readiness, incorporating the IT cum technology-oriented concepts in mathematics, will help sustain existing STEM growth here.

The aim of this quantitative cross sectional survey is to describe the frequencies of readiness of AI (Artificial Intelligence) in nursing education among undergraduate nursing students. Methodology of this research included, the design of this research is cross sectional descriptive study, sample size was N=50 undergraduate nursing students of first year first semester. Sampling technique was simple random sampling and setting was a Nursing College in private University. The data was analyzing by SPSS AMOS-23 software. The TAM (Technology Acceptance Model) was used to collect the data basically this tool was adopted from a Pakistani research article the validity and reliability of the tool has been mentioned in methodology section in chapter 3. A total of 50 undergraduate nursing students participated in the study examining readiness for the use of artificial intelligence (AI) strategies in nursing education. The demographic findings showed an equal distribution of male and female participants, with 25 (50%) students in each group. Regarding age, the majority of participants, 47 (94%), were aged 21–23 years, while 3 (6%) were aged 24–26 years. Regarding the perceived usefulness of AI strategies in nursing education, all participants reported negative responses to the statement that AI strategies improved their learning outcomes, with 26 (52%) strongly disagreeing and 24 (48%) disagreeing. For the statement that AI tools could help students understand complex nursing concepts, 18 (36%) strongly disagreed, 11 (22%) disagreed, 11 (22%) remained neutral, and 10 (20%) strongly agreed. Similarly, 42 (84%) participants disagreed or strongly disagreed that AI-based learning resources could improve their clinical decision-making skills, while 4 (8%) were neutral and 4 (8%) strongly agreed. Regarding whether AI strategies could make nursing studies more productive, 17 (34%) strongly disagreed, 12 (24%) disagreed, 11 (22%) were neutral, and 10 (20%) strongly agreed. All participants (100%) disagreed with the statement that AI tools could help them prepare more effectively for nursing examinations. The study revealed low readiness among undergraduate nursing students towards the use of AI strategies in nursing education. Most participants reported negative perceptions regarding AI usefulness, ease of use and integration into academic activities. The findings highlight the need for structured AI literacy training, practical guidance and education on the responsible use of AI. Further research with larger sample is recommended to explore student’s readiness for AI integration in nursing education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Real-Time Release Testing (RTRT) is an advanced pharmaceutical quality-assurance approach that enables product quality to be evaluated using real-time process data, in-process measurements, and validated analytical technologies. Unlike conventional end-product testing, RTRT focuses on building quality into the manufacturing process through continuous monitoring and control. The integration of Process Analytical Technology (PAT), Quality by Design (QbD), multivariate data analysis, automation, and advanced analytical techniques facilitates improved understanding and control of critical material attributes and critical process parameters. This review discusses the principles, implementation strategies, pharmaceutical applications, advantages, challenges, and regulatory aspects of RTRT. The major benefits include reduced testing time, faster batch disposition, improved process understanding, reduced product waste, enhanced manufacturing efficiency, and consistent product quality. However, implementation can be challenging due to high initial investment, instrument calibration and validation requirements, data integrity and cyber security concerns, skilled workforce requirements, regulatory expectations, and integration with legacy manufacturing systems. Regulatory frameworks from organizations such as the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), European Medicines Agency (EMA), and International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) provide a scientific and risk-based foundation for implementing RTRT. Future developments involving Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Digital Twins, Internet of Things (IoT), Big Data Analytics, and Industry 4.0 are expected to further enhance real-time quality monitoring and predictive manufacturing. RTRT therefore offers significant potential to modernize pharmaceutical manufacturing by enabling efficient, science-based, and continuous assurance of product quality.

Persistent AI agents can condition advice and correction on disclosures, histories, and inferred preferences. Apparent personalization fit is insufficient evidence of calibration. A system may misrepresent its user while the user poorly distinguishes accurate from inaccurate advice; their coexistence is termed dual miscalibration. Reciprocal miscalibration is a narrower hypothesis: representation-conditioned outputs affect behaviour, that behaviour updates the operative representation, and the updated state sustains or worsens both representation error and miscalibrated human reliance. The framework separates user-model fidelity, contextual representation fit, perceived fit, persuasive efficacy, and advice accuracy. An accurate record of a false user belief remains distinct from endorsing that belief as true. Performative prediction, preference pollution, persuasion profiling, distributed cognition, narrative railroading, and human-AI feedback research supply direct antecedents. The contribution is an operational refinement of these problems for conversational correction, with falsifiable propositions and interventions on representation updating and correction. Feedback to the human about independently checked outcomes is distinguished from behaviour fed back into the system. A factorial study tests immediate effects; a longitudinal intervention tests reciprocal reinforcement. Appropriate reliance additionally depends on payoffs, checking costs, relative competence, and learning opportunities. Neither reciprocity nor the benefit of the proposed controls has been established by this conceptual synthesis.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in embodied AI for robotic manipulation and planning, but their deployment in physical systems exposes vulnerabilities such as jailbreak attacks that induce unsafe behavior. Existing inference-time defenses are mainly evaluated on short instructions containing a single hazard, whereas realistic tasks may interleave safe and unsafe sub-tasks, conceal hazardous steps, or combine individually safe actions into unsafe outcomes. Such compound instructions make it harder for a single safety decision to distinguish hazardous sub-tasks from legitimate ones, risking either overlooking the hazard or rejecting the whole instruction. We introduce safe task completion, a task that requires an LLM-enabled robot to refuse the harmful part of an instruction while completing its legitimate part. To address this problem, we propose RuleGraph, a multi-agent Graph-of-Rules planning framework that distributes safety enforcement across multiple reasoning and verification stages. Five cooperating agents are used to ground general safety principles into world-specific rules, assess the instruction's sub-tasks in context, and derive a safe goal from the legitimate ones. Planning toward this goal is then organized as a graph of rule-specific nodes, where higher-level nodes inherit the union of their parents' rules, and candidate plans are progressively verified and aggregated until a single plan satisfies every relevant rule. In this way, RuleGraph reduces reliance on a single centralized safety decision. We evaluate RuleGraph on pure-attack and compound instructions across two benchmarks in two environments using Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). RuleGraph reduces ASR to 0% on both benchmarks while achieving the highest TSR among all methods, reaching 98.57% on the RoboGuard benchmark and 84.54% on our long-horizon compound instructions.

This paper presents a reinforcement learning based decision support system for adaptive pacing control in manual material handling tasks. Hand Activity Level optimization is formulated as a finite horizon Markov Decision Process, where actions select pacing intensities or micro breaks under stochastic object loads. Q-learning and Deep Q-learning are evaluated in simulation using productivity and cumulative ergonomic exposure metrics aligned with HAL-TLV guidelines. Results show that Deep Q-learning achieves higher productivity, but Q-learning has lower cumulative risk exposure.

BACKGROUND: Adverse drug events (ADEs) are a critical indicator of patient safety but are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. The potential of recent advances in natural language processing (NLP), particularly generative large language models (LLMs), to identify ADEs remains understudied. This study aimed to compare the performance of multiple LLMs in identifying ADE-Drug relationships in inpatient and ambulatory clinical notes. METHODS: We used clinical notes from the 2018 National NLP Clinical Challenge (n2c2) ADE dataset (inpatient; n = 505) and from outpatient encounters (n = 2555) between October 1, 2018, and December 31, 2019, at a large academic medical center based in New England. Notes were pre-processed into snippets for model input. Evaluated Models included: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.2-3B and their instruction fine-tuned variants (including low-rank adapters for Llama). Performance was assessed using both strict and relaxed evaluations (precision, recall, and F1) for all models, followed by manual evaluation (exact semantic match, partial match, missing ADE, drug mention only, not a drug, or wrong) of the two best-performing models. FINDINGS: Of the 1048 notes in the local test split, 450 (42.9%) contained at least one ADE. The n2c2 test set included 202 notes, of which 155 (76.7%) contained at least one ADE. GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini were the top-performing models among those evaluated. GPT-4o consistently outperformed GPT-4o-mini in ADE extraction across both datasets, with higher F1-scores (0.524 vs. 0.381) and a more balanced precision-recall profile. Both models captured ADEs effectively in explicit and complex clinical contexts, although limitations included misclassification of pre-existing allergies and occasional conflation of therapeutic indications with adverse effects. GPT-4o achieved higher exact match coverage and fewer errors across clinical notes, indicating more reliable performance in both inpatient and ambulatory settings. INTERPRETATION: This work establishes a foundation for integrating LLM methods into real-world drug safety surveillance, with direct implications for improving patient safety. FUNDING: None.

Drug repurposing, also known as drug repositioning or reprofiling, involves investigating existing drugs for uses beyond their original indications. Unlike traditional drug discovery, it utilizes existing information on pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, toxicology, clinical experience, and production, thereby reducing uncertainties in drug development. Advances in computational biology, systems pharmacology, artificial intelligence (AI), high-throughput screening (HTS), and omics sciences have transformed repurposing from an observation-based approach into a systematic strategy. Computational methods can identify drug–disease interactions through molecular targets, biological pathways, gene-expression profiles, and clinical phenotypes, which can be validated through experiments, data, and prospective studies. Integration with precision medicine enables approved drugs to be evaluated in patients selected by specific molecular or clinical features, while biomarker-based stratification may identify beneficiaries, particularly in heterogeneous disorders. Electronic health records and registries further provide real-world data for detecting treatment signals and evaluating drug effectiveness and safety in clinical practice. However, successful clinical implementation faces challenges, including incomplete or biased databases, computational prediction errors, and confounding and selection biases in clinical observations. Previous approval for one indication does not eliminate the need for indication-specific evaluation, as repurposing may require dose adjustment, additional safety testing, and clinical trials. Limited diversity in clinical databases may also restrict treatment generalizability. This paper reviews major repurposing approaches, including predictive modelling, transcriptomic analysis, screening, organoids, clinical data mining, and real-world evidence, emphasizing their integration with precision medicine and the criteria for successful clinical implementation.

Research on magnesium materials has achieved rapid development in 2025, with a total of 6124 related papers indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection, where China contributes 50.89% of the global output, occupying a leading position in international magnesium research. Bibliometric analysis indicates that microstructure evolution, mechanical performance, and corrosion resistance remain the mainstream research focuses of magnesium alloys. Meanwhile, functional magnesium material systems, including biomedical magnesium alloys, hydrogen storage media, and rechargeable magnesium batteries, have witnessed remarkable breakthroughs. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques are increasingly integrated into magnesium research workflows, supporting multi-performance forecasting, inverse alloy composition design and interpretable property regulation, which provides an innovative paradigm for the customized optimization of magnesium alloy properties. The continuous drop in primary magnesium prices further facilitates scaled industrial deployment of magnesium products. This review systematically summarizes the full spectrum of magnesium research advances in 2025 and highlights prevailing bottlenecks together with prospective research pathways for magnesium-based materials.

OBJECTIVE: Large language models are widely used in clinical care. Their reliability in specialized gynecological diseases such as premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) has not been fully verified. This study aimed to systematically evaluate and compare the accuracy and completeness of three mainstream large language models when answering standardized clinical questions about POI. METHODS: We developed 34 standardized questions covering five core domains of POI according to international clinical guidelines. Two senior obstetricians and gynecologists independently scored responses using a 5-point Likert scale. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using Cohen's kappa coefficient, intraclass correlation coefficient, and mean absolute error. Pairwise between-model score differences were computed and visualized using item-level heatmaps. RESULTS: All three models showed high and steady performance. Accuracy scores ranged from 4.59 to 4.84, and completeness scores ranged from 4.43 to 4.65. Inter-rater agreement was "good" to " excellent", with exact agreement between 91.18% and 97.06% and Cohen's kappa between 0.675 and 0.915. GPT-5.5 performed better in the area of clinical manifestations and treatment. DeepSeek-R1 showed greater stability, defined as maintaining consistently high scores with limited score fluctuation, in etiology- and counseling-related questions. Item-level heatmaps revealed that most individual-item differences were within ±0.5 points, whereas pairwise differences in overall mean scores fell within ±0.5, and some individual-item comparisons exceeded this range, with no obvious systematic bias. CONCLUSIONS: GPT-5.5, Claude Opus-4.7, and DeepSeek-R1 demonstrated favorable accuracy and completeness in answering standardized POI questions; overall performance was similar despite deviations across several individual questions. Item-level difference heatmaps further confirmed the consistency and reliability of the three models. These models can serve as reliable auxiliary tools for clinical information retrieval and patient education under professional supervision, meaning that all content generated by artificial intelligence must be checked by qualified clinicians before clinical use.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Liver transplantation (LT) is a uniquely curative treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), as it removes both the tumor and the underlying cirrhotic liver. However, organ scarcity makes candidate selection a central clinical and ethical issue. Over the past three decades, selection has evolved from simple morphologic thresholds toward increasingly multidimensional models of oncologic risk. AREAS COVERED: This review examines the evolution of selection criteria for LT in HCC, from the Milan criteria and subsequent morphology-based expansions to models incorporating tumor biology, serum biomarkers, treatment response, waiting-list dynamics, and artificial intelligence. The literature discussed includes landmark morphologic criteria, AFP-based models, PIVKA-II and AFP-L3 integration, downstaging strategies, dynamic scores such as TRAIN and NYCA, and machine-learning models including MoRAL-AI, TRIUMPH, and TRAIN-AI. EXPERT OPINION: The field is moving from categorical eligibility rules toward individualized, continuous risk estimation. Future selection should not aim merely to expand transplant access, but to identify patients most likely to achieve durable oncologic benefit. Artificial intelligence, radiomics, liquid biopsy, and multi-omic profiling may refine risk prediction, but their clinical adoption will require prospective validation, transparency, calibration, transportability, and integration into allocation systems.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: We study whether frontier large language models (LLMs) exhibit prospect-theoretic framing patterns in risky choice and how their risk posture compares with – and shapes – that of humans in business-relevant contexts. In two preregistered between-subjects discrete-choice experiments, a panel of 17 LLMs and 1029 human participants evaluated four numerically equivalent gain–loss framing scenarios, chose between a certain option and a probabilistic one, and provided a brief justification. Most frontier reasoning and chat models favored certainty in 87%–100% of trials across frames and contexts, substantially attenuating the classic gain–loss reversal, while lighter-weight models exhibited greater human-like framing sensitivity and, in some cases, extreme risk-seeking. Human participants reproduced the classic framing effect with modest variation across scenarios. When shown a “committee of advisors” recommendation aggregated from the first experiment, however, human choices shifted sharply toward certainty in both frames – by 8.3 to 15.5 percentage points in the gain frame and 25.1 to 37.3 in the loss frame, controlling for risk preferences and other factors. Topic modeling of justifications shows that unadvised humans drew on moral and responsibility-based reasoning essentially absent from LLM output; under AI advice, that vocabulary receded and certainty- and probability-based language expanded – humans began to sound like the LLMs. Deploying an LLM as a decision aid is thus not a neutral upgrade: it imports a model-specific distribution of risk recommendations and delegates not only the choice but the framing of the decision itself, with direct implications for AI governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The adoption of robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) across multiple specialties has outpaced procedural specific evidence of benefit over laparoscopy. The question we seek to answer is not whether RAS "works"- rather whether the purported advantages are primarily for the surgeon or the patient and under what circumstances those advantages justify the added cost and complexity. With the review of randomized, trials, large comparative cohorts, cost analyses, and ergonomic studies, we hope to highlight areas where RAS delivers patient-centered value compared to surgeon benefits. Across many routine operations, with well-performed laparoscopy, patient outcomes are largely equivalent, however operative time, cost, and emerging potential safety concerns highlight the importance of a measured approach to the spread of RAS. There is evidence that RAS does offer some benefits, namely in deep pelvic dissections. Surgical approach should be based on documented outcomes, surgeon proficiency, and surgeon benefits rather than being driven by platform availability alone.

The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions. Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model's general capabilities.

PharmBench is a bilingual (Turkish–English) benchmark for evaluating the safety of large language models (LLMs) in community-pharmacy medication counseling. Eleven model configurations are assessed on 40 language-specific scenarios (20 clinical cases presented in Turkish and English) spanning five high-alert medications and four clinical archetypes. Each response is scored against an expert-derived safety checklist by a four-model LLM jury with cross-family routing, and summarized by a Severity-Weighted Safety Score (SWS). Jury judgments are validated against an independent licensed pharmacist. This record contains the frozen model responses and jury scores, the scenario bank with scoring checklists, derived result tables, publication figures, and the analysis notebook and figure-generation scripts. All tables and figures can be reproduced from the archived artifacts without any API access; a full re-run against the live provider APIs is also supported. Source code is released under the MIT License and data under CC BY 4.0.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Evaluating a fine-tuned coaching model with expert graders is slow and expensive, and an LLM judge cannot be trusted without ground truth. We present a staged pipeline that screens candidate LLM judges and student models before expert review, using explicit decision rules at each stage: judge output audit, similarity with hosted judges, bias checks, and decision robustness. We demonstrate it on an AI dental hygiene coach. The case study uses synthetic, clinically unvalidated training and reference data to demonstrate the operation of the pipeline, rather than to establish the clinical performance of the resulting models. Two fine-tuned small language models (Granite-4.1-8B and Qwen3-8B), each trained at three data sizes, were scored on seven metrics by five judges (three local, two hosted). Two local judges, Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, were not distinguishable from the agreement between the hosted judges on six of seven metrics by rank correlation, and Qwen3.8-27B was the most similar to the hosted judges overall. No judge met our criterion for favoring its own model family or training-data source. The student comparison did not separate the two models on any metric under the pipeline's rule, so the choice of Granite-4.1-8B, which led in 29 of 35 judge-by-metric cells, is a lean that depends partly on truncated Qwen3-8B outputs. The pipeline also surfaced problems that raw scores hid, including the truncated outputs and hallucination flags from one hosted judge that no other judge corroborated. No dental hygiene expert has graded these responses, so the findings are preliminary and the pipeline's final stage, anchoring to expert judgement, is proposed but not performed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study explores the attitudes and level of readiness of secondary education teachers regarding the integration of ChatGPT into teaching. Adopting a mixed-methods approach utilizing a questionnaire, the study examined a sample of teachers from two schools in Central Macedonia. The findings reveal an attitude of cautious optimism. Participants acknowledge the tool"s significant utility in lesson preparation and material creation, which saves valuable time. However, they express strong concerns regarding the reliability of information, ethical issues, the absence of a regulatory framework within schools, and the risk of undermining students" critical thinking. In conclusion, although artificial intelligence is envisioned as a future digital assistant, there is an urgent need for systematic and experiential institutional training for teachers to ensure its pedagogically safe utilization.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract The rate at which collaborative robots (cobots) are evolving from isolated, pre-programmed manipulators into collaborative partners that operate productively alongside humans, other robots, and machines is accelerating rapidly. Advances in computer vision is enabling cobots, even in dynamic and cluttered settings, to detect, recognise and assess both environment and actions. However, achieving higher detection accuracy and real-time localization in dynamic systems remains a challenge, as most existing approaches assume uncluttered backgrounds with limited scene complexity. Closing this gap is critical for both research and industrial deployment. This paper reviews the development of visual perception in cobots, surveys emerging computer vision algorithms, and examines a holistic perception pipeline in which raw vision signals, vision language models (VLMs), and augmented/virtual reality interfaces jointly power a unified sense-think-act loop. The review finds that cobots in high-mix, reconfigurable factories face serious challenges: occlusions in fields of view, fluctuating illumination, ambiguous backgrounds, few- or zero-shot object scenarios, high-speed motion, and computational problems in fusing heterogeneous data streams in real time. Cobots also need to manipulate damaged items, requiring vision algorithms that infer geometry from sparse cues and support adaptive grasping. Finally, the review identifies three complementary research directions to unlock plug-and-play cobots: (1) information aware sensor-fusion pipelines transmitting only credible voxels to reduce bandwidth while preserving sub-millimetre accuracy; (2) language conditioned planning and control networks mapping plain-language goals to smooth, jerk-bounded trajectories; and (3) pre-trained few-shot reward heads that score task progress without bespoke metrics, closing the reinforcement learning (RL) loop. Combined, these advances promise cobots that can be commissioned with relatively few demonstrations.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Intent-Based Networking (IBN) is a key enabler of autonomous network management in next-generation networks, as it allows operators to drive the network through high-level intents instead of low-level configuration commands. In this paper, we propose a semantic routing framework for telecom intent classification and translation across the radio access networks (RANs), transport, 5G core, and cloud/edge domains. This framework operates locally to preserve intent privacy and avoid the latency and cost of cloud-based Large Language Model (LLM) solutions. The proposed framework is composed of intent classification and translation. To accurately classify the intent, we propose fine-tuning sentence-transformer models using contrastive learning over a 3GPP TS 28.312-aligned taxonomy of five top-level routes and 22 branches, supported by a telecom-specific codebook of 1,100 intents. In addition, we develop a branchaware, template-driven rule-based module for intent translation that enforces deterministic, hallucination-free parameter extraction and explicit missing-field detection, ensuring a structured and verifiable output pipeline. The numerical results show that the best fine-tuned encoder achieves up to 99.02%/94.61% route/branch classification accuracy, outperforming both base encoders and a commercial embedding baseline. The proposed translator achieves up to 96.24% translation accuracy, compared to 85.37% for a cloud-based LLM benchmark. Moreover, since the proposed pipeline runs entirely on local hardware, an average translation latency of 4.81 ms is recorded against 4,163.58 ms for the cloud-based benchmark, i.e., a speedup of approximately 866x.

Road tunnels are indispensable components of transport networks, providing critical connections while operating continuously under demanding environmental, geological, and hydrogeological conditions. Their large dimensions, confined geometry, and uninterrupted operation make comprehensive inspection challenging. Full-face inspection technologies such as light detection and ranging (LiDAR) can rapidly capture high-resolution surface data; however, the resulting digital models are often descriptive rather than explanatory or instructive. This limitation is critical because seemingly minor defects may indicate latent deterioration and, if untreated, can lead to severe safety and operational consequences. With advances in artificial intelligence, particularly large language models (LLMs) and robotic inspection platforms, tunnel inspection is expected to move beyond defect detection towards knowledge-driven diagnosis and decision support. This paper presents a serviceability-oriented Prescriptive Twin framework for road-tunnel maintenance, that is, a digital twin that represents asset conditions and recommends maintenance actions from inspection evidence and codified engineering knowledge. The framework connects inspection data, prescriptive knowledge, decision-making, and verification through a Web Ontology Language (OWL 2) domain ontology populated by a schema-guided LLM pipeline. The ontology integrates tunnel maintenance standards, road asset data requirements, and an extended Construction Operations Building Information Exchange (COBie) schema, while the pipeline converts narrative standards into expert-validated seven-level Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) chains. A multimodal layer maps red–green–blue (RGB), RGBD (RGB with depth), thermal, and ground-penetrating radar (GPR) outputs to causal-chain entry points, such as level 4 indicators and level 5 causes. The framework specifies an identity-resolution rule that binds observations from different modalities, and from successive inspection cycles, to a persistent defect instance, and a governance layer that binds every decision threshold to a dated clause of a specific standard edition, so that a prescription can be reconstructed against the edition under which it was issued. Chain traversal maps onto the inspection report and an inter-cycle change report. Demonstrated on two defects in an operating road tunnel, the framework generates traceable prescriptions and shows how multimodal evidence improves intervention accuracy: at the worked example, thermal and GPR evidence escalated the intervention tier and expanded the repair scope by a factor of 3.2 relative to RGB-only inspection, delivering an industry-deployable pathway for standards-compliant maintenance decision support.

This study examined the relationship between skills-based education practices and perceived employability competence among final-year undergraduates in three state-owned universities in Ondo State, Nigeria, while drawing comparative lessons from the United Kingdom. A descriptive survey and correlational design were used. Data were obtained from 460 final-year students selected through multistage sampling using the Skill-Based Education Practices and Graduate Employability Questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, Pearson product-moment correlation and multiple regression were used. Documentary analysis was used for the United Kingdom component. Skills-based education practices were significantly and positively related to perceived employability competence (r =.695, p <.001). The six dimensions jointly explained 61.9% of the variance in perceived employability competence (R =.786, R² =.619, adjusted R² =.614), F(6, 453) = 122.87, p <.001. Work-based learning (β =.272), university–industry collaboration (β =.230), vocational and technical skills training (β =.145), practical/project-based learning (β =.136), and entrepreneurship education (β =.122) made significant positive contributions. Career guidance and employability training had a positive but non-significant unique contribution (β =.101, p =.189). The findings indicate the need to strengthen structured workplace learning, employer engagement, practical training and entrepreneurship while improving career development provision. UK practices provide useful principles, but adaptation to Nigerian institutional and labour-market conditions is necessary.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly proposed as a decision-support layer inside operational management systems, yet many such systems disclose neither the provenance of their recommendations nor a mechanism by which a manager can govern their consequences before they take effect. This chapter addresses that governance problem through SmartTransit OS, a prototype public-transit operating system built and examined here as a governance testbed rather than as a finished management product. The system unifies four role-scoped portals — Passenger, Driver, Administrator/Operations, and System Operations Center — around one authentication system and one shared operational state. Software events are communicated in real time, but vehicle telemetry is simulated. Server-enforced, field-level role-based access control governs what each role may see and change. Every automatically generated decision-support output, covering estimated arrival time, occupancy, and operational anomalies, carries an explicit provenance label identifying it as a rule-engine, hybrid, database, or simulation output, and authorized personnel may review recommendations, with decisions recorded in an audit log. The prototype does not enforce completion of review and does not execute recommendations automatically; any operational change requires a separate authorized human action. The chapter argues that the decision-support layer's current deterministic, rule-based design is a deliberate methodological choice: it isolates the governance mechanisms — authorization, shared state, provenance, human approval, and auditability — from the additional uncertainty a trained model would introduce, allowing their specified behavior to be examined separately before any such model is introduced. The demonstration dataset is small and seeded, and the prototype has not been integrated with real GPS/AVL hardware, GTFS-Realtime feeds, ticketing systems, or external transit operators; no field deployment or independent security audit has been conducted. Evaluation is architectural and qualitative, supplemented by author-reported synthetic boundary-case counts that do not measure operational performance. The chapter concludes that this governance pattern does not depend on the underlying decision-support method and would remain relevant if future versions of the system introduce trained models for prediction, anomaly detection, or dispatch.

Social media and artificial intelligence (AI) are changing the way agricultural information is shared in India; however, research on these two tools of communication has not been reviewed together. The present review examined the publication profile of Scopus-indexed research on social media and AI in Indian agricultural communication, the way this research has studied the two tools, and what the evidence shows about them. Following PRISMA 2020, Scopus and OpenAlex were searched for the period 2010–2025, and every eligible study was checked for Scopus indexing one by one. Out of 2,735 records, 33 studies were included, coded by tool, research design, theme and actor, and synthesised narratively. The research is very recent, as 82% of the studies appeared in 2021–2025. Sixteen studies examined social media, mainly WhatsApp, 14 examined AI, mainly machine-learning analysis of Kisan Call Centre queries, and three applied AI to agricultural tweets. Content and data analytics was the most common design (52%), and none of the studies was a randomised trial. Scopus indexed 54% of the eligible AI studies but only 14% of the eligible social media studies. Farmers preferred WhatsApp and familiar tools and created as well as received content, whereas AI was mostly used to analyse farmers' questions and was rarely tested with farmers. The review concludes that the evidence is recent, descriptive and thin on effects, and that future research should test both tools with farmers in the field.
