Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly moving beyond analytical retail functions into product development, raising new questions about how consumers respond depending on where AI is positioned within the process. Across three studies with U.S. consumers in fashion-related contexts, this research examines how the task AI performs and how its role is framed shape consumer responses to products developed with AI involvement. Study 1 maps consumers’ perceptions of fashion-related tasks along a logic–intuition continuum and identifies trend forecasting as a logic-oriented task and design as an intuition-oriented task. Study 2 compares AI involvement in these two contrasting product-development tasks and finds lower purchase intention when AI is involved in design rather than trend forecasting, with heightened human identity threat accounting for part of this difference. Study 3 focuses on the intuition-oriented design context and shows that framing AI as complementing rather than replacing human designers is associated with lower identity threat and higher purchase intention. Together, the findings suggest that consumer responses depend not only on whether AI participates in product development, but also on where AI is positioned within the process and how its contribution relative to human creativity is framed. This research advances understanding of task-dependent responses to AI by identifying human identity threat as a mediator linking AI involvement to purchase intention and by showing how role framing can shape purchase intention when AI participates in creative work.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Protocol for a cross-sectional meta-research audit of how public datasets used to develop artificial intelligence (AI) for neurosurgery report patient demographics and data origin. The frame comprises 110 datasets: the 84 unique datasets catalogued by Chan et al. (J Clin Med 2025) and 26 pre-specified, widely used datasets. Fourteen items are extracted from each descriptor paper, including age, sex, race/ethnicity, socioeconomic status, country of data origin and inclusion of children. A large language model produced a first-pass extraction with verbatim quotes. Two investigators verify every item independently and reconcile any disagreements, and two further reviewers double-extract a random 20% sample. Countries are mapped to World Bank income groups. This record time-stamps the protocol, codebook, sampling frame and analysis code before human verification began. The AI outputs and verification workbooks are withheld until verification is complete, to keep the second reviewers blind.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The global nursing shortage remains critical, making the successful transition and retention of newly graduated nurses (NGNs) essential. Informed by Duchscher’s Transition Theory, which highlights the transition shock experienced by newly graduated nurses, and Walker et al.’s work readiness framework, newly graduated nurses often face significant stress when entering clinical practice. Work readiness is critical for addressing the challenge, yet its trend and stage-specific influencing factors have not been systematically examined. This study aims to explore the potential trend and influencing factors of work readiness among NGNs in China during their first year of employment. An exploratory longitudinal mixed-methods study. During the quantitative phase, 200 NGNs completed the Chinese version of the Work Readiness Scale for Graduate Nurses (WRS-GN) at entry(T0), 4 months (T1), 8 months (T2), and 12 months (T3). Changes in work readiness were examined using repeated-measures analysis of variance. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured focus group interviews with 16 participants and analyzed using content analysis. Work readiness varied significantly over time (F = 14.11, p < 0.001), following a “rise–decline–rise” pattern. The largest improvement occurred from T0 to T1. Work readiness showed a numerical but not significant decline from T1 to T2, coinciding with reduced organizational awareness and motivation amid department shifts and independent night shifts, as well as increased workload and stress. Readiness improved again from T2 to T3 as professional identity and confidence strengthened. Qualitative data explained these trends, showing that intrinsic motivation and multilayered support helped early adaptation, while independent practice and reflection later promoted role transformation. Work readiness among newly graduated nurses demonstrates a nonlinear, stage-specific, and differentiated developmental pattern during the first year of employment. Tailored educational and managerial support is needed across transition stages, including early reinforcement of fundamental skills and supportive preceptorship, enhanced preparation for independent practice, organizational support and stress management during the mid-transition stage, and the promotion of reflective learning and career development planning in later stages, to facilitate a smoother professional transition. Such support may also have implications for retention.

Work-related musculoskeletal symptoms are common in physically demanding food-processing environments, yet salmon-processing workers in southern Chile remain under-characterized. This cross-sectional field study characterized 100 full-time workers from a salmon-processing facility in Puerto Montt, Chile, and identified candidate predictors of self-reported regional pain. Participants completed surveys on demographics, work history, lifestyle, psychosocial, and sleep-related factors; anthropometrics and grip strength were also measured. Binary outcomes captured 12-month self-reported pain in the low back, shoulder, and upper extremity. Pain prevalence was high across regions: low back 52%, shoulder 44%, and upper extremity 50%. Sparse learning methods, including LASSO and the Sparse Wrapper AlGorithm, were applied within logistic regression models to reduce a broad biopsychosocial feature set. Sleep-related variables recurred across pain outcomes, while anthropometric and physical-capacity measures appeared more region-specific. Findings support data-driven, field-oriented screening strategies for applied ergonomics surveillance.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Auditing LLM agents against policies is critical to ensure safety but requires rereading long trajectories once per policy. Can we instead record each trajectory once and reuse that record for policies not known in advance? We propose write once, check many, a framework in which a writer model converts each agent trajectory into a policy-independent ledger of the agent's actions and outcomes. A reader then checks each new policy against the ledger alone, without access to the original trajectory. On 900 trajectories from SHADE-Arena, $τ$-bench, and $τ^2$-bench, we show that a 12B reader of narrative ledgers can either match or in fact achieve higher AUC than the same 12B model reading full trajectories. On SHADE-Arena policies that combine several facts, our approach outperforms a 31B model reading the trajectory (.777 vs. .713 AUC). When checking eight SHADE-Arena policies separately, ledgers use about $5\times$ fewer tokens, including the cost of writing them. A deeper analysis shows that rule-based extraction performs better on some single-action policies, and ledgers can miss evidence in long tool outputs and message contents. Our results suggest that reusable, policy-independent records can make retrospective agent auditing more efficient and effective, and highlight important considerations in ledger design.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. This representation combines compact free-form text with sparse images to preserve semantic content and complementary visual details across temporal scales, supporting temporal navigation without a fixed semantic schema. A Writer encodes each video once by consolidating overlapping multiscale observations, and a Reader retrieves and organizes evidence solely from the resulting memory. With the underlying models frozen, we evolve their workflows and operators using distinct feedback: query-independent source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, and QA failures in evidence localization and utilization for the Reader. Experiments support this separation for generalization beyond development queries, with our evolution strategy improving average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While reducing storage by about 99.86% on average relative to raw videos, Video-EMem improves Qwen3-VL-30B by an average of 2.6% across three long-video QA benchmarks over direct input of 2,048 frames. Using the same o3 answer model as the state-of-the-art agentic method, it improves average accuracy by 2.5% with lower per-query latency.

Semantic segmentation depends heavily on real images with pixel-level annotations, making dense supervision a major obstacle to deployment in new domains. We study task-specific data-free semantic segmentation, where training uses generic pretrained generative priors but has access to no target-domain images, masks, or captions--only a predefined category set. We introduce Zero-Data Semantic Segmentation (ZeroDSS), a feedback-driven approach that treats synthetic supervision as an adaptively controllable training distribution rather than a direct surrogate for real data. ZeroDSS constructs a semantically structured prompt distribution through LLM-guided compositional generation and adaptive class rebalancing, then converts the prompts into image-mask pairs using diffusion attention. Its feedback-driven distribution refinement consists of a two-phase closed-loop training procedure with a single loop-back step. In Phase I, a segmenter is trained using confidence-weighted supervision and dual-scale consistency. In Phase II, model feedback is used to adaptively target underperforming categories and refine diffusion-derived masks using model predictions. After this refined initial training, a teacher-student framework is utilized in the final phase to iteratively improve the fused supervision and segmenter through exponential moving average (EMA) updates. Using synthetic training data only, ZeroDSS achieves 35.0% mIoU on MS COCO with DeepLabV3, and 66.3% and 63.5% mIoU on PASCAL VOC with DeepLabV3 and Mask2Former, respectively. These results show that explicitly constructing and iteratively refining the synthetic supervision distribution can substantially reduce the synthetic-to-real gap in dense prediction.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

Workers due to there Immense Work and Dedication to There Field as a Government Employee.The most common cause of chronic pain under the heel in adults is plantar fasciitis (PF), which accounts for documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: International recruitment is used to address nursing workforce shortages, yet recruitment alone does not ensure successful integration into destination healthcare systems. This study aimed to explore how internationally recruited nurses (IRNs) experience and make sense of workplace integration in Saudi Arabia, with attention to the organizational, relational, and experiential processes that shape integration over time. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study with reflexive thematic analysis was conducted with 19 IRNs in three tertiary hospitals in southern Saudi Arabia. Participants were purposively recruited, and data were generated through semi-structured interviews. Organizational Socialization Theory (OST) was used as a sensitizing theoretical framework rather than a predetermined coding structure. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Four interrelated themes captured participants’ integration experiences: (1) Entering the Workplace with Limited Organizational Preparation; (2) Becoming Integrated Through Workplace Relationships; (3) Learning the Unwritten Workplace Through Experience; and (4) Integration as an Uneven Trajectory Over Time. Formal preparation and orientation were often limited, shifting substantial responsibility for workplace learning to peers, supervisors, and experiential exposure. Supportive relationships facilitated learning and belonging, whereas harsh interactions, perceived inequities, and variable organizational support complicated integration. Conclusions: Workplace integration was experienced as a gradual, relational, and uneven process rather than a discrete orientation event. Healthcare organizations have a central responsibility for supporting integration, while informal peer learning should complement rather than replace structured organizational support.

Measuring AI by how much faster developers work is like judging electricity by how much faster it spun a steam-era factory. A fuller measure asks what new work becomes possible. We surveyed 331 software developers at Microsoft about what AI lets them do that they could not do before and analyzed their answers using reflexive thematic analysis with a human-in-the-loop, multi-model AI council. Developers described doing familiar work faster (Faster, 45%), undertaking work previously beyond their reach (Further, 36.9%), and taking on new kinds of work centered on building for and directing AI agents (Afresh, 12.4%). Across these accounts, learning and scaffolding ran in both directions: developers learned new skills with AI while externalizing their tacit knowledge as the context and standards that guide AI's work. Drawing on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, we frame developers and AI as joint learners whose zones meet at the skill-judgment nexus: AI can supply skill faster than it can reliably judge its own work, and developers must continuously bridge that gap. Whether they do sets them on one of two paths. On one, developers' judgment grows alongside AI's skill, and they codify what they learn so the loop keeps turning. On the other, they become hollow orchestrators, approving work they can no longer judge and losing the identity and meaning they once drew from it. Based on our findings, we offer a two-way scaffolding playbook to help developers, teams, and tool builders take the first path.

What the Web community believes about toxic conversations, such as that toxicity rises in longer and deeper threads, was measured mostly with Google's Perspective API, which is shutting down; large language models (LLMs) will make the next measurements. We find that LLM labelers mistake second-person address for toxicity, and that this one bias manufactures laws that human labels do not show. On 1.25 million news comments with crowd labels, Claude Haiku flags 12% of the non-toxic comments that contain no "you" and 51% of those with four or more; a single crowd rater flags 6% and 10%. Deeper replies address someone more often, so under Haiku toxicity rises with reply depth (+0.93 percentage points per level), while under the crowd's labels it slightly declines (-0.12). Rewriting "you" in the third person removes two thirds of the false rise; flagging only as many comments as the crowd does not remove it, and showing Haiku the parent comment enlarges it. All seven LLMs we test over-flag "you", and at the crowd's flag rate, without the parent, any false rise of the open ones vanishes at a fixed number of second-person words; Haiku also over-flags "you" on Reddit, Gab and Wikipedia talk pages. Agreement with human labels does not reveal the bias: we prove that a fixed Cohen's kappa leaves a law nearly unconstrained. We therefore certify the law instead of the labeler. Threadsafe uses the labeler's scores to choose which comments human raters label and to predict the others, and corrects the predictions with the human labels; linear laws are estimated without bias whatever the labeler does. In simulated audits its intervals for the laws keep nominal coverage from 250 labels on, where uniform-sample methods such as PPI++ fall short, and at 1,000 to 8,000 labels are 0.75 times as wide as those of design-based supervised learning (DSL); a thousand human labels rule out Haiku's rising law.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background: Polymyxins remain important therapeutic options for the treatment of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacterial infections; however, their clinical application is limited by a narrow therapeutic window and a high risk of nephrotoxicity. Although research on polymyxin-associated nephrotoxicity has expanded rapidly in recent years, the overall evolution of research themes, knowledge structure, and emerging frontiers in this field remains unclear. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the development trends and research hotspots of polymyxin-induced nephrotoxicity using bibliometric analysis. Methods: Relevant publications on polymyxin-induced nephrotoxicity published between January 1, 2005, and November 13, 2024, were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection database. CiteSpace and VOSviewer (Baxter Healthcare Corporation) were used to analyze publication trends, authorship, institutional and country collaboration networks, keyword co-occurrence, clustering, and burst detection. Results: A total of 569 publications were included in this study. The annual publication output demonstrated an overall increasing trend, indicating increasing attention to polymyxin-associated nephrotoxicity research. Li Jian was the most productive author, Monash University was the most productive institution in terms of publication output, and the United States contributed the highest number of publications among all countries. Keyword analysis revealed that research themes have evolved from early characterization of nephrotoxicity and clinical safety assessment toward the identification of acute kidney injury risk factors, elucidation of oxidative stress-related mechanisms, pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic optimization, and development of individualized dosing strategies and nephroprotective approaches. Burst analysis further indicated increasing attention toward biomarkers, precision dosing, and novel therapeutic strategies. Conclusion: Bibliometric analysis revealed that research on polymyxin-induced nephrotoxicity has progressively evolved from toxicity characterization to mechanistic exploration and precision management. Current challenges include an incomplete understanding of interactions among nephrotoxic pathways, limited dynamic prediction models, and insufficient clinical translation of emerging protective strategies. Future research should focus on integrating multi-omics approaches, artificial intelligence-based risk prediction, therapeutic drug monitoring, and safer polymyxin formulations to optimize the balance between antibacterial efficacy and nephrotoxicity prevention.

University presses face converging pressures from scholarly quality, peer-review integrity, reviewer scarcity, Open Science, artificial intelligence, international visibility, and economic sustainability. This article proposes Epigenetic Editorial Intelligence, a bioinspired conceptual framework that represents stable institutional rules as Editorial DNA and models operational adaptation through epigenetic regulation, an Artificial Immune System, organizational memory, human–AI collaboration, and multiobjective optimization. Nine operational indicators are formalized and aggregated into a Global Editorial Intelligence Index (GEII). Internal model behavior is examined through paired synthetic ablations that disable one mechanism at a time, using 200 Monte Carlo repetitions, common random-number streams, 95% confidence intervals, alternative weighting schemes and 1000 Dirichlet weight perturbations. Results are interpreted as structural-consistency diagnostics rather than empirical validation. This work provides a reproducible conceptual and mathematical foundation for subsequent implementation and testing with real editorial records.

topics: Mathematical and Theoretical Epidemiology and Ecology Models

documents.abstract: The successful integration of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms in precision agriculture provided farmers with the means to identify potential issues, such as early disease detection or pest infestations, by making crop-related predictions. The new technological developments in this field improve the functioning of traditional agriculture by reducing the dependence on specialized human expertise and facilitating greater access to diagnostic procedures. However, most studies conducted in this area rely on centralized training of AI models, which leads to increased costs and raised privacy-related concerns. Federated learning (FL) offers a compelling framework for collaboratively training machine learning (ML) models on distributed datasets without centralizing the data owned by each participant. FL offers significant advantages in the preservation of data privacy, facilitates the collaborative exploitation of geographically distributed data sources, and reduces the risks associated with centralized collection. In this paper, we investigate the current limitations and performance boundaries of existing Federated and privacy-preserving learning in distributed sensing systems for plant disease detection, in scenarios that closely resemble real-world conditions. Our analysis specifically examined how FL aggregation algorithms, such as FedAvg, FedAvgM and FedProx, work in a custom multi-client experimental setup where data is partitioned so that each participant observes only those symptom patterns associated with specific environmental and climatic conditions. We propose further partial aggregation of the local model, an approach where we send only the model backbone to the central server, while the classification head of each participant remains strictly on the client side. The construction of environmentally heterogeneity is combined with a globally representative stabilizer node designed to preserve knowledge across disease classes that may be absent from certain clients.

Introduction: Diagnostic otology relies on operator-dependent interpretation of otoscopy, temporal bone computed tomography (CT), audiometry and vestibular testing, and diagnostic accuracy outside specialist settings remains suboptimal. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed as a scalable decision-support solution, but its pooled accuracy, robustness beyond development data, comparative value against clinicians and barriers to clinical implementation have not been synthesised across all diagnostic otology modalities. This review aimed to quantify the diagnostic performance of AI across otoscopic, radiological, audiological and vestibular applications and to map opportunities and barriers to implementation. Methods: The study strictly adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Randomised controlled trials, cohort, case–control and cross-sectional diagnostic studies (prospective or retrospective) evaluating an AI index test against a clinical reference standard were eligible; systematic reviews were excluded from synthesis. Risk of bias was appraised with QUADAS-2 supplemented by QUADAS-AI considerations. Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity were pooled on the logit scale using random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood with modified Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman confidence intervals) with 95% prediction intervals (PI); risk differences (RD) quantified AI–clinician comparisons. Subgroup analyses, meta-regression, influence diagnostics, small-study tests and GRADE certainty assessment were performed. Results: Of 139 unique records, 64 primary studies (2019–2026; otoscopy 37, temporal bone CT 14, audiology 6, vestibular 7) were included. No randomised trial of an AI diagnostic tool in otology was identified. Pooled internal-validation accuracy was 92.5% (95% CI 90.0–94.5) (k = 36; PI 64.7–98.8%; I² = 97.8%, τ² = 0.858): otoscopy 93.2%, temporal bone CT 90.2%, audiometry/tympanometry 97.6% and vestibular testing 84.0% (between-modality P = 0.003). Pooled sensitivity and specificity were 92.6% (95% CI 89.4–94.8) and 89.5% (95% CI 74.3–96.1), respectively (diagnostic odds ratio 105; summary AUROC 0.957). Accuracy fell to 81.2% (95% CI 59.1–92.8) in external, prospective or point-of-care cohorts (P = 0.026 versus internal validation), and studies using surgical, histopathological or objective reference standards reported lower accuracy than those using expert annotation (89.0% vs 93.6%; P = 0.041). Task-specific AI outperformed clinicians on identical cases (RD +18.2 percentage points, 95% CI 7.3 to 29.0), and AI assistance increased clinician accuracy (RD +9.4 points, 95% CI 1.4 to 17.4), whereas general-purpose multimodal large language models underperformed specialists (RD -25.0 points). Of 47 meta-analysed studies, 34 (72.3%) had at least one high risk-of-bias domain; certainty of evidence was low to very low. Discussion: Task-specific AI achieves high diagnostic accuracy across diagnostic otology and consistently exceeds non-specialist performance, supporting its role as a triage and decision-support adjunct, particularly in primary care, tele-otology and resource-limited settings. However, extreme heterogeneity, wide prediction intervals, performance attenuation under domain shift, spectrum and reference-standard bias, scarce prospective evidence and the absence of outcome trials constitute the principal barriers to implementation. Conclusion: AI is a promising but not yet implementation-ready component of diagnostic otology. Multicentre prospective validation with surgical or objective reference standards, standardised image acquisition, transparent reporting (STARD-AI/TRIPOD+AI-aligned) and pragmatic randomised trials measuring patient-important outcomes are required before routine deployment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: We investigate whether trade openness, governance, environmental taxation and selected macroeconomic indicators can classify the contemporaneous CO2 emission level of countries observed over 2000 to 2023, using data from the World Development Indicators and the OECD. CO2 emissions per capita are divided into three ordinal levels, low, medium and high, using tertile cut points estimated on the training data only within every validation split. Four classifiers, Random Forest, XGBoost, a support vector machine and a multinomial logistic regression, are tuned and compared alongside two models designed specifically for ordinal outcomes, an ordered logistic regression and an ordinal decomposition of XGBoost, under four validation designs: a country grouped holdout and country grouped 5 fold cross validation, in which no country appears in both the training and test sets; a chronological holdout; a 1 year ahead forecasting task; and a random stratified country year split, retained only as a reference point. Under country grouped cross validation, no classifier achieves a decisively higher accuracy than the others: nested cross validation gives a mean accuracy of 0.644 for XGBoost, 0.648 for Random Forest, 0.671 for the support vector machine, 0.674 for the multinomial logit, 0.676 for the ordered logit and 0.637 for the ordinal XGBoost model, with overlapping confidence intervals throughout. This is markedly lower than the 0.91 accuracy obtained under a random country year split with the same tuned pipeline, a gap of 12.5 percentage points for XGBoost, confirming that a substantial part of the high accuracy obtainable under random splitting reflects the model recognizing previously seen country profiles rather than generalizing to unseen countries. Accuracy falls less sharply under the chronological holdout and the 1 year ahead forecasting task, in the region of 0.65 to 0.74, indicating that the classifiers generalize better across time within a country than across countries. Permutation importance, SHAP and LIME consistently identify government effectiveness, urban population growth and environmental tax revenue as the features most strongly associated with model predictions, with a moderate contribution from trade openness and the smallest from GDP growth, a ranking that is stable across importance methods, learning algorithms and cross validation folds. These variables are predictors of the model's output, not estimated causal determinants of emissions, and the results are best read as evidence for climate risk monitoring and further policy evaluation rather than as a causal policy assessment.

Abstract The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) is revolutionizing industrial processes by interconnecting sensors, machines, and computing resources to enable intelligent automation, real-time monitoring, and predictive maintenance. Despite its potential, efficient allocation and management of resources in IIoT networks remain a significant challenge due to the dynamic, heterogeneous, and large-scale nature of industrial environments. Traditional static or heuristic resource allocation methods often fail to satisfy conflicting objectives such as minimizing latency, maximizing throughput, ensuring energy efficiency, and maintaining system reliability. To address these challenges, this paper presents the design and development of an AI-based multi-objective resource management system for IIoT systems. The system integrates reinforcement learning (RL) for adaptive, real-time decision-making with Harris Hawks Optimization (HHO) for multi-objective optimization, balancing competing performance metrics across sensing, communication, computing, and control layers. The RL agent predicts system states and dynamically adjusts resource allocation, while HHO fine-tunes the solutions to achieve optimal performance under multiple constraints. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms conventional static and heuristic approaches, achieving higher efficiency, faster adaptability, and improved scalability. By intelligently managing resources and optimizing system behavior, this system enhances overall operational reliability and Quality-of-Service in IIoT networks. The results indicate that combining AI-driven decision-making with advanced nature-inspired optimization provides a robust and efficient solution for next-generation industrial applications, paving the way for more intelligent, resilient, and resource-efficient IIoT systems.

Text classification is a widely studied problem in information retrieval and data mining, with applications ranging from healthcare diagnosis to the detection of COVID-19-related fake news. Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated text, and the rapid spread of misinformation during the pandemic has made automated fake news detection an important task. In this study, we apply pretrained transformer-based transfer learning (TL) models and large language models (LLMs), namely BERT-base, ALBERT-base, XLM-RoBERTa-base, DistilBERT, GPT-2, XLNet, and T5, to the COVID-19 English Tweets dataset, which contains 6,420 tweets labeled as real or fake. To further improve performance, we apply six late-fusion optimization techniques: weighted fusion, particle swarm optimization (PSO) fusion, the Nelder-Mead algorithm, Powell's method, the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm, and trust-region constrained optimization. Models are evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, and confusion-matrix heatmaps are used to visualize the predictions of each model. GPT-2 achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 0.9631, precision of 0.9612, recall of 0.9610, and F1-score of 0.9600, while Nelder-Mead fusion achieved the best result among the fusion methods with an accuracy of 0.9610. These results highlight the value of LLMs for COVID-19 fake news detection. We conclude by outlining future directions, including multiclass classification, multilingual datasets, and real-time social media streams.

Future sixth-generation (6G) Internet of Everything (IoE) networks require zero-touch management systems capable of autonomously allocating communication and computational resources, satisfying service-level constraints, and providing transparent explanations for their decisions. Existing neuro-symbolic explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) twins improve interpretability by coupling neural prediction with symbolic reasoning; however, most rely on statically engineered causal graphs, fixed rule sets, and immutable knowledge bases. Such closed-world assumptions are unsuitable for non-stationary 6G environments in which radio conditions, mobility patterns, interference relationships, and service requirements continuously evolve. To address this limitation, this paper proposes LL-NS-XAI, a Lifelong Learning Neuro-Symbolic XAI Digital Twin for zero-touch 6G IoE management. The framework integrates three tightly coupled planes: an online implicit learner at the physical edge for time-varying service association and uplink/downlink resource allocation; a dynamic explicit learner in the virtual core for directed acyclic graph (DAG)-based Bayesian reasoning, most-probable-explanation inference, and explainable trust scoring; and a meta-cognitive layer that monitors reasoning residuals, detects parameter drift, structural drift, and ontological emergence, and autonomously revises the causal graph, probabilistic rule sets, conditional probability tables, and knowledge base. Unlike static neuro-symbolic twins, LL-NS-XAI treats realized post-decision outcomes, including achieved channel quality indicator (CQI), measured end-to-end delay, and throughput, as interventional evidence for online causal-model adaptation. Experimental evaluation using a non-stationary 5G-derived dataset with injected parameter drift, structural drift, and emergent IoE service classes demonstrates that LL-NS-XAI maintains higher long-term trustworthiness, lower reasoning residuals, and bounded performance degradation compared with static XAI twins, non-stationary bandits, and pure continual-learning baselines. The framework additionally accommodates a previously unseen IoE service class through autonomous causal-graph expansion, recovering near-oracle performance without offline retraining. These results demonstrate that lifelong causal adaptation can improve the robustness, explainability, and autonomy of AI-enabled zero-touch management in evolving 6G IoE networks.

Abstract Large language models (LLMs) show promise for extracting clinically meaningful information from unstructured health records, yet real-world deployment is constrained by limited scalable, trustworthy validation approaches. Conventional evaluation relies on annotation-intensive reference standards and incomplete structured data, limiting population-scale use. We propose a multi-stage validation framework for LLM-based clinical information extraction that enables rigorous assessment under weak supervision by integrating complementary validation strategies. The framework combines prompt calibration, rule-based filtering, semantic grounding, judge-LLM evaluation, expert review, and predictive validity analysis to quantify uncertainty without exhaustive manual annotation. We applied this framework to extract substance use disorder (SUD) diagnoses across 11 substance categories from 919,783 clinical notes. Rule-based filtering and semantic grounding removed 14.59% of LLM-positive extractions that were unsupported or structurally implausible. For high-uncertainty cases, the judge LLM showed substantial agreement with subject matter expert. Using judge evaluations as references, the primary LLM achieved an F1 score of 0.80. LLM-extracted SUD diagnoses predicted subsequent engagement in SUD specialty care more accurately than structured-data baselines. By unifying complementary validation strategies, this work presents a generalizable human-in-the-loop framework for establishing the trustworthiness of LLM-based clinical information extraction at scale while minimizing the need for exhaustive manual annotation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Neonatal late-onset sepsis (NS) is a life-threatening condition driven by a dysregulated host response to infection, where neutrophil dysfunction plays a pivotal role. Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), as the frontline sensors of the innate immune system, are increasingly recognized as key regulators of immune cell function, yet their specific connection to neutrophil biology in NS remains largely undefined. Objective This study aimed to decode a novel PRR-neutrophil (PRRN)-associated molecular signature in NS. Methods Bulk transcriptomic data from NS peripheral samples (GSE138712) were analyzed using Limma, WGCNA, and CIBERSORT to identify shared PRRN-related differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Hub genes were narrowed down via PPI network analysis. A diagnostic model was constructed using 132 machine learning algorithms on the training set (GSE69686, NS peripheral blood bulk profile) and validated on an independent set (GSE25504, NS peripheral blood bulk profile) based on PRRN-associated hub genes. SHAP analysis identified the central hub gene in training set. Single-cell RNA sequencing data of sepsis patient peripheral blood(GSE167363) were used to validate its cell-specific distribution, functional trajectory, and regulatory network at spatial and temporal manners via cutting-edge analytical framework. AI-based drug screening (DrugReflector) and molecular docking computationally nominated a candidate therapeutic compound for NS targeting PRRN-associated central hub genes. Finally, NS patient clinical samples were collected for the validation of expression patterns of hub genes. Results We identified PRRN-associated diagnostic and candidate therapeutic models for NS patients and nominated GSR as the PRRN-associated and up-regulated hub gene in NS pathogenesis. Single-cell analysis confirmed that GSR is predominantly expressed in neutrophils within the NS samples and is enriched in pathways related to innate immune response. Conclusion This study systematically defines novel PRRN molecular co-expression patterns in NS, establishing GSR as a neutrophil-centric hub gene. These findings offer a potential diagnostic framework and an exploratory therapeutic target for NS patients, and the candidate compound requires further experimental validation.

Healthcare professionals experience substantial burden when providing long-term care for patients with Parkinson’s disease. Despite their central role in care delivery, the experiences of healthcare professionals remain under-examined in Indian healthcare contexts. This qualitative study explored professional caregiver burden among healthcare professionals involved in Parkinson’s disease care in South India. Twelve healthcare professionals (Neurologists, Nurses, Physician Assistants, Physiotherapists, and Psychologists) were recruited from two tertiary hospitals in Chennai between April and May 2025. A semi-structured interview schedule was utilised to gather data. Data were analysed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis. The study identified 5 major themes (1) Emotional Burden of Continuous Care in PD, (2) Clinical and Cognitive Complexity, (3) Critical Care and Physical Demands, (4) Family Dynamics and Relative Challenges, and (5) Administrative and Systemic Barriers, encompassing 18 sub-themes. The findings indicate that professional caregiver burden in PD care arises from the interaction of cultural expectations, structural constraints, and the progressive nature of the disease. Remarkably, accumulated clinical experience did not diminish cognitive burden; instead, greater experience escalated exposure to therapeutic uncertainty and prognostic complexity. Findings associated with physical rehabilitation are presented as an illustrative case, due to the single-participant illustration of the physiotherapy discipline. The professional caregiver burden among healthcare professionals in PD care operates across multiple professional and systemic dimensions. It also represents a patient-safety concern with implications for occupational health policy and institutional mental-health support in tertiary care settings. These burden dimensions elucidate how professional caregiver burden, emerging from progressive neurological disease care, is shaped by structural constraints and cultural care contexts.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping educational practices, requiring teachers to develop new competencies while navigating complex ethical considerations. This qualitative study explores the perceptions, practices, and orientations of 28 Lebanese schoolteachers regarding the integration of AI in school settings. Findings indicate that while a majority of participants reported familiarity with AI, only a limited proportion integrated AI into their instructional practices. Reported barriers included insufficient training, lack of institutional support, and concerns related to data privacy and ethical use. The analysis led to the identification of three qualitative orientations toward AI integration—reluctant users, early adopters, and critical skeptics—reflecting differentiated levels of readiness and engagement. The findings highlight the need for context-sensitive, pedagogically grounded, and ethically informed professional development to support sustainable AI integration in education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Riverine (fluvial) flooding remains a significant climate-related disaster in many countries. Extreme rainfall events caused by climate change cause significant damage and disruption to communities living near riverbanks or neighboring land areas, particularly when risk-sensitive development is ignored. This necessitates an effective mechanism to predict river flooding events and provide timely early warnings to the most vulnerable populations in high-risk flood-prone areas. The dynamics of flood risks require a localized, automated, and scalable solution that can be centrally monitored. This study presents a river flood forecasting system integrating artificial intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT). This system was deployed in one of the flood-prone river basins in Sri Lanka to assess the operational feasibility of real-time hydrological monitoring and flood-risk classification. The proposed system employed two machine learning models, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), for flood-risk prediction and IoT sensors (rainfall and ultrasonic sensors) for real-time hydrological data collection. The machine learning models were developed using rainfall, discharge rate, and river water level data to predict flood-risk states. A rule-based ensemble strategy was implemented by combining the outputs of LSTM and XGBoost to prioritize positive-class detection and reduce missed positive-labeled observations. Model performance was evaluated primarily using recall for the positive flood cases, while the overall accuracy was reported as the complementary metric alongside positive-class recall, providing an overall assessment of classification performance. Among the evaluated input window configurations using the same chronological holdout, the rule-based ensemble model with a 1-day input window showed the most favorable observed balance of performance metrics, achieving 100% positive-class recall, with 98.73% accuracy, 50.00% positive-class precision, and 66.67% positive-class F1-score. The 100.00% recall was based on correctly classifying all four positive-labeled observations in the held-out test set (4/4; 95% exact binomial CI: 39.8%−100.0%) and these observations occurred consecutively from November 25 to 28, 2024, and represent one continuous positive-labeled flood episode. The proposed safety-oriented AI-IoT framework demonstrates the operational feasibility of integrating real-time sensing with AI-based flood forecasting; however, longer-term field deployment, including actual flood events, is required to evaluate flood-event prediction performance under real-world flood conditions.

Women's safety applications have increasingly adopted mobile sensing, Global Positioning System (GPS), cloud services, and artificial intelligence to support emergency communication and risk awareness. However, existing systems differ considerably in their methods of detecting emergencies and responding to them. Some applications primarily provide manual SOS functions and location sharing, while others introduce voice activation, contextual risk assessment, offline communication, predictive analysis, or evidence collection. This paper reviews recent technology-based women safety and emergency response systems, with particular attention to their emergency triggers, use of artificial intelligence, location services, evidence collection, communication mechanisms, and limitations. The reviewed literature covers mobile applications, predictive safety systems, contextual monitoring, and cloud-supported emergency platforms. The analysis shows that current solutions have improved the speed and accessibility of emergency assistance, but several systems remain focused on individual functions rather than integrated risk detection and response. Important gaps remain in continuous behaviour analysis, anomaly detection, automatic triggering, reliable operation under limited connectivity, evidence management, and reduction of false alarms. Based on these observations, the paper discusses a proposed research direction for an integrated AI-based women safety platform designed to combine predictive risk assessment, multiple emergency triggers, location tracking, evidence collection, and automated emergency response.
topics: IoT and GPS-based Vehicle Safety Systems

documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare, driven by the increasing availability of electronic health records (EHRs), medical imaging systems, genomic data, and wearable devices, has created significant challenges related to patient privacy, data security, and regulatory compliance. Traditional centralised machine learning (ML) approaches often require large-scale data sharing, which increases the risk of sensitive medical information exposure. Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising distributed learning paradigm that enables collaborative model training across multiple institutions without transferring raw patient data. Recent advances in privacy-preserving FL have further strengthened its applicability in healthcare through the integration of techniques such as differential privacy (DP), homomorphic encryption (HE), secure aggregation, blockchain-assisted frameworks, and secure multi-party computation. This study critically reviews recent developments in privacy-preserving FL for healthcare applications published between 2024 and early 2026, with particular emphasis on medical imaging, EHRs analytics, genomics, and wearable health monitoring systems. In addition, major technical and security challenges, including non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data distributions, communication overhead, scalability issues, gradient leakage, model poisoning, and membership inference attacks, are comprehensively analysed. Regulatory, ethical, and interoperability concerns associated with cross-institutional collaboration are also discussed. Finally, current research gaps, emerging trends, and future directions for developing secure, scalable, and trustworthy federated healthcare systems are identified.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: As an important vehicle for resource integration in the construction of new power systems, the virtual power plant (VPP) has moved from the demonstration and pilot stage into a critical transition period of standardized construction and market-oriented operation. This paper systematically reviews the technological development trajectory and the practical progress of VPPs in China. At the technical level, key advances are reviewed across three core domains: resource perception and adjustable potential assessment; optimal dispatch and control strategies (covering centralized, distributed, and reinforcement learning-based methods); and cloud–edge–terminal platform architecture and information security. At the practical level, the paper traces the policy evolution from the early demand response pilots to the 2025 Guiding Opinions on Accelerating the Development of Virtual Power Plants, surveys grid-led and third-party-aggregator demonstration projects, and analyzes business models and pathways for participation in electricity markets. On this basis, the key challenges facing Chinese VPPs in technical standardization, market access, regulatory frameworks, and data security are analyzed, and international experience from Europe (Next Kraftwerke, Flexitricity), North America (FERC Order 2222), and Australia (Tesla VPP) is summarized. Finally, future development pathways are discussed from four directions: technological trends (digital twins and the integration of large language models), the improvement of market mechanisms, the construction of the policy and standards system, and the cultivation of a multi-stakeholder industrial ecosystem.

Alumni–student engagement has evolved from static communication into a dynamic, data-driven ecosystem. Traditionalalumni management platforms primarily focus on event coordination and record maintenance, but lack personalization, intelligence, and adaptive interaction. Recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) enable the automation of mentor– mentee matching based on skills, interests, and professional attributes, thereby enhancing the relevance and quality of alumni–student interactions. This paper reviews existing alumni engagement systems, identifies key technological limitations, and emphasizes the growing need for AI-based recommendation mechanisms within academic ecosystems. While visualization dashboards continue to support transparency and performance tracking, AI-driven recommendations emerge as the core enabler of personalized engagement. The paper integrates insights from contemporary literature and proposes a conceptual direction for building intelligent, scalable, and institution-centric engagement platforms.

Predictive maintenance reduces unexpected machine failures and downtime by continuously observing equipment condition and identifying abnormal behaviour before severe failure occurs. This review paper examines recent research on Digital Twin (DT), artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, multi-sensor condition monitoring, and predictive maintenance of industrial machines, with emphasis on induction motors. Based on the reviewed literature, a low-cost integrated architecture is proposed using temperature, vibration, current, and RPM sensing, an ESP32 controller, AI-based fault prediction, Digital Twin updating, and IoT-based monitoring. Random Forest is considered as the main classification model because related literature demonstrates strong performance for motor-fault classification. Sample formulas for RMS vibration, mean, variance, RPM, and percentage change are presented. The proposed workflow connects physical sensing, data processing, AI prediction, virtual representation, alert generation, and predictive-maintenance decision support. Illustrative graphs are included only as sample results and must be replaced by measured experimental data before final validation.

A 2026 study reports that sentiment classifiers score higher on reviews rewritten by small language models than on the human originals, by up to 5.8 accuracy points, and reads the gain as stylistic alignment: the rewrite strips idiosyncrasy and hands the classifier text closer to what it was trained on. It concludes that benchmarks cleaned or paraphrased by language models will overstate classifier performance. Two older literatures point the other way. Paraphrase and style-transfer attacks drive the same classifiers down, and a 2025 study of fifty thousand rephrased tweets finds that rewriting pulls sentiment toward neutral, a pull its robustness checks found again when the prompt asked for the sentiment to be kept. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that neither direction measures the classifier alone, because every one of these designs scores the rewritten text against the label of the text it replaced. The paper separates four accounts of a rewrite-induced gain: alignment of style with the classifier's training data; a fall in the rate of neutral predictions, which the anchor's scoring counts as errors; the paraphraser acting as an annotator that decides the polarity and then writes it plainly; and the removal of hard, mixed and ironic items. It shows from the anchor's released code that its prompt demands one of two polarities and that a neutral prediction is always scored wrong, that its own count of label flips is mislabelled: the printed 291 is the net gain, not the number of improvements, and that a test-time rewriting study found rewritten inputs still sitting with the out-of-distribution data in embedding space. The paper consolidates the measured values in two tables and a figure, states a licensing procedure as an algorithm, counts from the anchor's released predictions that a fall in neutral predictions carries about half of the largest gain, and names the re-annotation, paraphraser-baseline and prompt-ablation controls that would settle which account holds for the rest.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, but its outcome-level rewards provide only sparse supervision. On-Policy Distillation offers dense token-level feedback, yet requires a stronger compatible teacher, while on-policy self-distillation relies on hand-designed privileged information. We observe that the MoE architecture itself offers a way to resolve this dilemma, as increasing the activation budget per token exposes latent expert capacity and yields a potentially stronger teacher within the model. However, naive expansion degrades performance because newly co-activated experts are not optimized to work together. We therefore propose MoEvolve, a bidirectional distillation framework following a recovery-then-improvement strategy: we first restore the activation-expanded high-$k$ model and further strengthen it by exploiting its additional active capacity, then reverse the direction of distillation to transfer the enhanced capabilities back into the original low-$k$ configuration, retaining its inference-time activation budget. Across diverse MoE models and benchmarks, MoEvolve improves the initial models by up to $22.2$ domain-average points and outperforms same-budget RLVR baselines by up to $6.5$ points. Notably, the final low-$k$ models often surpass their activation-expanded teachers.

As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes higher education, learning support centers are uniquely positioned to intentionally assess whether if and how to best integrate AI tools into academic services. This session presents a 6-week project framework that was designed to: • Review the literature on critical AI literacy and training • Benchmark current best practices in AI policy, use, and integration alongside human-centered academic services • Examine student AI knowledge and use (needs assessment) • Identify and evaluate relevant AI tools or platforms The framework was developed within the Academic Success Center (ASC) at Nevada State University where Center peer educators (student employees) served as project leads and evaluators. This model offers a practical, research-informed pathway for institutions seeking to lead responsibly in AI-integrated learning support or other student services. Session activities include a walkthrough and discussion of the model structure, tools, challenges, and recommendations. Attendees will leave with: (1) a sample 6-week project roadmap, (2) a student-centered model for AI evaluation and pilot design, (3) learning frameworks grounded in critical AI literacy, (4) adaptable resources for assessment and decision-making, and (5) strategies for positioning students as co-creators in institutional/unit change
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Introduction With the deep integration of digitalization and generative artificial intelligence, artificial intelligence has transformed from a mere technical tool into a core collaborative partner within modern workplaces and human‑resource management. As an interdependent human‑AI working mode characterized by complementary task division, joint task accomplishment, complementary decision‑making, and continuous iterative interaction between employees and AI agents, AI‑employee collaboration is conceptually distinct from simple AI adoption, instrumental AI use, and AI‑assisted technical systems. Drawing on social cognitive theory, the present study aims to investigate how AI‑employee collaboration predicts employee innovation behavior, alongside the mediating role of self‑efficacy and the moderated‑mediation boundary condition of servant leadership. Methods Three‑wave time‑lagged questionnaire data were collected from 259 employees working in internet‑service, finance, and catering industries across Beijing and Jinan. Hierarchical regression and bootstrap approaches were adopted to test the proposed moderated‑mediation model. Results The results show that AI‑employee collaboration exerts a significant positive predictive effect on employee innovation behavior. Self‑efficacy partially mediates the relationship between AI‑employee collaboration and employee innovation behavior. Moreover, servant leadership positively moderates the link between AI‑employee collaboration and self‑efficacy and further strengthens the indirect predictive effect of AI‑employee collaboration on employee innovation behavior through self‑efficacy. Discussion This research enriches existing literature by providing incremental empirical evidence for the internal cognitive mechanism and contextual boundary of AI‑driven employee innovation. Theoretically, it unpacks the cognitive “black box” connecting AI‑employee collaboration and employee innovation and identifies servant leadership as a key situational contingency factor. Practically, these findings deliver concrete, actionable managerial insights for digitally transforming organizations to leverage AI tools and unlock employees’ innovative potential.

The study “A Study on the Influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Literacy on Career Readiness Among Young Adults in Chennai” aims to establish a connection between the level of awareness about AI and career readiness. The influence of artificial intelligence is increasing in all fields of activity, especially in the educational and professional spheres. Therefore, understanding the characteristics of this technology is becoming a vital skill for achieving employability in the future. The study uses a descriptive research design, with a primary data collection method. The data was gathered by distributing questionnaires among one hundred respondents who were selected using a convenience sampling technique. The data analysis involved the percentage analysis of the results, the weighted average of the responses, multiple linear regression, and Pearson’s correlation. The analysis focused on investigating the level of AI literacy, the factors that contribute to it, and the relationship between AI literacy and career readiness. The results of the study showed that the mean score for AI literacy is 3.61, while that of career readiness is 3.33. According to multiple regression analysis, such variables as peer, social, and professional interaction, and personal curiosity and self-learning were statistically significant predictors of AI literacy, with a score of approximately 66%. The results also showed that AI literacy and career readiness were positively correlated (r = 0.819, p < 0.001). The study established the significance of improving the level of knowledge and skills about artificial intelligence among young adults, which will increase their chances of being employed. This information can be useful for academic organizations and young people who intend to gain knowledge about AI to enhance their employability.

ABSTRACT The rapid proliferation of latency‐sensitive and data‐intensive applications has accelerated the adoption of cloud–fog computing architectures to support real‐time processing and distributed resource management. However, efficient task scheduling in cloud–fog environments remains a challenging problem because of resource heterogeneity, dynamic workloads, network variability, and stringent quality of service (QoS) requirements. Artificial intelligence (AI)‐based techniques, including machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), deep reinforcement learning (DRL), and hybrid AI approaches, have emerged as promising solutions for addressing these challenges. This paper presents a systematic review of AI‐based task scheduling techniques in cloud–fog computing environments published between 2021 and 2025. Following a PRISMA‐inspired methodology, 74 high‐quality studies were selected and analyzed. The reviewed works are classified into ML, DL, DRL, and hybrid AI‐based scheduling categories and evaluated with respect to scheduling objectives, QoS parameters, datasets, evaluation tools, and implementation environments. The analysis reveals that AI‐driven scheduling approaches significantly improve key performance metrics, including task scheduling performance (14%–90%), latency reduction (15%–65%), energy optimization (15%–41%), load balancing (20%–45%), execution time reduction (15%–45%), and cost optimization (10%–32%). This review further highlights the increasing adoption of DL, DRL, and hybrid AI techniques for managing complex and dynamic cloud–fog infrastructures. Additionally, this study identifies critical research challenges, including scalability, resource heterogeneity, lack of standardized benchmark datasets, limited real‐world deployments, and insufficient consideration of network‐layer dynamics. Finally, emerging research directions and future opportunities for developing scalable, adaptive, and intelligent scheduling frameworks in cloud–fog computing environments are discussed. This article is categorized under: Technologies > Cloud Computing Technologies > Internet of Things Technologies > Artificial Intelligence

Despite the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled web applications for Japanese language learning, existing platforms suffer from three critical challenges: insufficient integration of AI capabilities with pedagogical design, limited scenario adaptability across proficiency levels, and suboptimal lightweight deployment on the browser side. To address these gaps and explore instructional design patterns tailored to diverse Japanese learning needs, this study focuses on web application technology implementation and interaction design as the core analytical dimensions. Three typical AI-enabled Japanese tutoring web applications were selected as research objects, and 192 Japanese learners participated in the empirical research. Quantitative data were obtained through technical disassembly, questionnaire surveys, and web-based behavior tracking; learning effects were verified by comparative experiments, and the weight of instructional design elements was determined via the analytic hierarchy process, finally extracting core instructional design modes suitable for the mainstream Japanese learning stages from beginner to upper-intermediate (Japanese-Language Proficiency Test [JLPT] N5–N2), with preliminary applicability discussion for the advanced stage (N1 and above). The results show that web-based lightweight AI technology deployment and real-time AI interactive feedback design are the core elements, with a combined weight of over 40%. There is a significant positive correlation between web-based AI technology implementation and user satisfaction, with the highest implementation effect and user acceptance in listening, speaking, and grammar modules. Compared with traditional Japanese web learning platforms, AI-enabled instructional design can improve learners’ listening and speaking abilities by 58.0%(M=58.0,SD=4.2,95% CI [56.4, 59.6], Cohen’s d=1.82, large effect), grammar analysis abilities by 46.5% (M=46.5,SD=5.1,95%CI [44.8, 48.2], Cohen’s d=1.45, large effect), and enhance learning sustainability by 85.7% (M=85.7,SD=6.3,95%CI[83.5,87.9], Cohen’s d=2.01, large effect), based on N5–N2 learner data with robust statistical power. Three core instructional design modes were identified, adapted to zero-based-N4 fragmented learning, N3–N2 systematic learning, and N1+ immersive learning, respectively. This study clarifies the core elements and optimization direction of such applications, providing standardized and practical theoretical references and paths for their design, development, and teaching practice.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The use of accurate vision models for crop monitoring, disease diagnosis, and plant phenotyping in agriculture is hindered by the lack of expertly annotated data, especially in developing countries. We propose A100, an agricultural vision foundation model that is pre-trained using self-supervised learning on 3 million unlabeled images from fields covering more than 100 crop species. A100 uses a hybrid CNN-Transformer backbone that fuses MBConv stages for local feature extraction with Transformer stages for global contextual representation. A100 uses pre-training with the integration of DINO self-distillation, iBOT masked patch reconstruction, and KoLeo uniformity regularization, resulting in features that are better than ImageNet-12K supervised representations for agricultural applications without any fine-tuning. By utilizing a frozen backbone, the accuracy for crop classification of A100 is 95.37%, which is +2.56% better than ImageNet-12K, and reduces the leaf count error by 10.4% on the GroMo25 phenotyping benchmark, proving that the same backbone can be used for classification and regression tasks. After full fine-tuning, the performance of A100 is 99.90% on 32-class crop identification and 99.02% on 44-class disease detection. On the difficult PlantDoc dataset, A100 outperforms all baselines, such as CvT-13 (64.89% against 63.56%). Remarkably, A100 obtains 98.01% accuracy on plant classification using just 1% of the labelled data (about 284 images per category), showing great label efficiency for use cases with limited labeling. Under an identical protocol, A100 also outperforms the publicly released agricultural foundation models FoMo4Wheat and LeafVision by more than 14 points at 1% labels. We plan to publicly release our pretrained model to allow agricultural professionals to adapt A100 for various plant analysis applications using limited annotations.

Developing a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) that is accurate for the specific conditions under which it will be applied, rather than simply for the predefined configurations chosen by the model developer, is a significant challenge in atomistic simulation. Active learning (AL) addresses this challenge by closing the loop between candidate generation, data selection, reference calculation, and model updating. Here, we survey more than seventy studies, with an emphasis on work from 2020 to 2026, to understand how active learning has evolved from a niche, on-the-fly training technique for query-by-committee and Gaussian process force fields into a diverse family of data-efficient strategies. he reviewed examples include on-the-fly molecular dynamics, active data selection for fine-tuning pretrained models, kernel- and representation-based acquisition using frozen pretrained models, and reaction-aware sampling for chemical systems far from equilibrium. We explore the use of active learning in elemental and alloy mechanics, hydrogen and ion diffusion, ferroelectrics and effective Hamiltonians of functional materials, reactive and photochemical dynamics, high-entropy and compositionally disordered materials, as well as generative and autonomous material discovery pipelines. Drawing on a growing body of critical, methodologically self-aware literature, we also show that this achievement carries systematic caveats. Uncertainty estimates are not interchangeable across model architectures and are frequently the least reliable exactly where they matter most. We close by discussing the outlook for standardized, uncertainty-calibrated, and observable-targeted active-learning workflows in the foundation-model era.

Research and development into artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applications in crop management are hindered by a lack of suitable public datasets. Whereas applications in disease and pest detection benefit from a comparatively higher amount of available data, applications like water-deficit stress detection often have very few if any public datasets available. Moreover, most datasets that are available are single-modality and frequently RGB-only, leaving the early detection and enhanced performance offered by other methods, and particularly by multimodal approaches, out of reach. Datasets with accurate metadata, higher numbers of plants, and smaller intervals between data points are also scarce. To address this, we publicly release ADA 2025, a >500 GB comprehensive multimodal dataset of young sugar beet plants under healthy and water-deficit conditions combining thermal, hyperspectral, RGB, and depth imagery along with relevant environmental and metadata and both relative water content (RWC) and leaf thickness as ground truth sources. Exemplary results showcase the dataset's validity in terms of differences detectable between stressed and healthy plants.

Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have significantly improved the ability to operate real-world software through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) using visual observations and natural language instructions. However, maintaining strong performance on unseen applications remains challenging, as practical tasks often require long-horizon procedural knowledge and application-specific operation patterns. In addition, constructing executable tasks and collecting corresponding trajectories for training still heavily rely on human-annotated data, incurring substantial cost. In this paper, we propose MAGE (Manual-augmented computer use AGent Execution and learning), a framework that leverages user manuals as a scalable source of procedural knowledge to improve both inference and training. During execution, MAGE retrieves task-relevant manual content and uses a planner to generate explicit procedural guidance for CUAs. To further account for the discrepancies between manuals and actual GUI environments, such as version differences or user settings, MAGE also adapts the agent policy through environment interaction. During training, MAGE converts manuals into executable task-plan pairs and uses the plans to guide environment rollouts toward task-relevant states; the resulting trajectories are then used to optimize the policy without human-authored demonstrations. This unified design enables effective utilization of manuals for both task execution and training, reducing reliance on human-authored training data. Experimental results across six applications demonstrate improvements in task success rates over strong baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of manual-guided planning and policy adaptation in new software environments. We provide the code and reproduction scripts at https://github.com/ku-autoai/MAGE.
